docs.title: django-spec-mcp
docs.text:
Serve django-service-specs services and selectors as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, conforming to MCP 2026-07-28 and 2025-11-25 (Streamable HTTP).

Coming from drf-mcp?

This package is djangorestframework-mcp-server moved onto the kernel. Moving from drf-mcp lists what a project has to change, starting with the live state its first deploy drops.

docs.title: What this is
docs.text:
django-service-specs is the kernel: a Django project declares each operation once as a spec. A ServiceSpec is a mutation, a side-effecting callable; a SelectorSpec is a read. The spec carries what the operation takes (a Validator, or reads declared as Parameters), who may run it (its permissions, kernel PermissionChecks), and what it returns (a Presenter), and the kernel's dispatch runs it the same way for every transport.

django-spec-mcp is the MCP transport over those specs. It mounts a single /mcp endpoint that speaks Streamable HTTP per the MCP spec, and registers your specs as MCP tools and resources. The endpoints are plain Django views, and the unit of registration is the spec, not a view.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Reach for this package when:

  • Your project declares its operations as django-service-specs specs (or is about to) and you want to expose them to an MCP-aware client (Claude Desktop, Inspector, Cursor, etc.).
  • You want a single, spec-compliant /mcp endpoint with pluggable auth (an MCPAuthBackend for the authorization server you run) and a small surface that you can audit.
  • You don't want to rewrite your service layer in a parallel framework.

Skip it when you don't need the MCP wire format — call your services directly.

docs.title: What ships
docs.text:
• Tools — tools/list, tools/call for register_tool, over a kernel ServiceSpec (mutations) or SelectorSpec (reads, with an optional FilterSet, ordering and pagination). register_tools registers every spec in a kernel SpecRegistry.
  • Resources — resources/list, resources/templates/list, resources/read against a kernel RETRIEVE SelectorSpec; RFC 6570 templated URIs whose variables are the spec's reads.
  • Prompts — prompts/list, prompts/get against render callables returning strings, PromptMessages, or async coroutines.
  • Discovery — server/discover, the 2026-07-28 revision's replacement for the initialize handshake. Answered without a session, so a modern client can lead with it.
  • Argument completion — completion/complete against per-argument completers on prompts and resource templates.
  • Pluggable auth — an MCPAuthBackend verifies the bearer token; AllowAnyBackend (dev only) ships, and bearer_challenge builds the 401 challenge a backend of your own answers with. A tool or resource is guarded by its spec's own kernel permissions, and scopes= at registration adds an OAuth scope gate.
  • RFC 8707 audience binding through audience_matches, which a backend calls; RFC 9728 PRM served from the configured backend.
  • Per-binding rate limits — MCPRateLimit Protocol with FixedWindowRateLimit, SlidingWindowRateLimit, and TokenBucketRateLimit implementations shipped.
  • Async POST/DELETE + GET-side SSE push — sync urls for WSGI, async_urls for ASGI; MCPServer.notify(session_id, payload) pushes JSON-RPC frames on the session's SSE stream. Per-worker InMemorySSEBroker or cross-worker RedisSSEBroker (behind [redis]); Last-Event-ID resume via InMemorySSEReplayBuffer / RedisSSEReplayBuffer.
  • OpenTelemetry instrumentation — mcp.tools.call, mcp.resources.read, mcp.prompts.get spans (no-op without the [otel] extra installed).
  • Origin allowlist + protocol-version validation + session lifecycle per the transport rules of both revisions. 2026-07-28 and later declare version, identity and capabilities on every request and hold no session; 2025-11-25 and earlier negotiate once through initialize. Both are served concurrently on one endpoint, because a legacy client has no fall-forward mechanism.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install django-spec-mcp                              # base install
pip install "django-spec-mcp[redis]"                     # +Redis SSE broker for multi-worker ASGI
pip install "django-spec-mcp[otel]"                      # +OpenTelemetry instrumentation
pip install "django-spec-mcp[redis,otel]"                # everything

…or with uv:

uv add django-spec-mcp                                   # base install
uv add "django-spec-mcp[redis]"                          # +Redis SSE broker for multi-worker ASGI
uv add "django-spec-mcp[otel]"                           # +OpenTelemetry instrumentation
uv add "django-spec-mcp[redis,otel]"                     # everything

Optional extras degrade gracefully:

  • RedisSSEBroker / RedisSSEReplayBuffer raise a clear ImportError from __init__ if redis isn't installed.
  • The OTel tracing helper yields a no-op span when opentelemetry-api isn't importable, so handlers stay branch-free.
  • filter_set= on a selector spec needs django-filter, which the kernel's filter extra installs; nothing else here imports it.

  • Concepts — tools vs resources, sessions, tool results, origin allowlist.

docs.title: Async deployment
docs.text:
MCPServer exposes two URL trees that mount the same registries, auth backend, and session store. Pick one based on infrastructure:

Mount Use when server.urls (default) WSGI, mixed sync/async work, simplicity server.async_urls ASGI, high-concurrency workloads, async-native services

Both speak the same MCP wire format — clients cannot tell the deployments apart. The difference is internal: async_urls dispatches I/O-bound handlers through arun_service / arun_selector so a single Python process can serve many concurrent MCP calls without a thread pool.

docs.title: Switch to ASGI
docs.text:
urls.py
from django.urls import path

from invoices.mcp import server

urlpatterns = [
    # Sync: path("mcp/", server.urls),
    path("mcp/", server.async_urls),
]

Run with an ASGI server:

uvicorn myproject.asgi:application
# or
daphne -b 0.0.0.0 -p 8000 myproject.asgi:application
# or
hypercorn myproject.asgi:application --bind 0.0.0.0:8000

A standard myproject/asgi.py from django-admin startproject works without modification — Django's get_asgi_application() happily serves async views.

docs.title: Middleware
docs.text:
Both mounts sit outside Django's browser-session machinery, because MCP is a bearer-token transport with no CSRF token and no login page to redirect to:

  • CsrfViewMiddleware — the endpoint is csrf_exempt, so POST and DELETE are not rejected for a missing token.
  • LoginRequiredMiddleware (Django 5.1+) — the endpoint sets login_required = False; authentication is the MCP auth backend's job, and an unauthenticated call gets a JSON 401 with a WWW-Authenticate challenge rather than a 302.

Everything else in MIDDLEWARE applies normally.

docs.title: Sync collaborators are bridged automatically
docs.text:
AsyncStreamableHttpView, the plain async Django view async_urls mounts, accepts the same auth backend and session store as the sync view. Sync methods on those collaborators are wrapped in asgiref.sync.sync_to_async at the call site, so the existing AllowAnyBackend, InMemorySessionStore, and DjangoCacheSessionStore work unchanged.

If you write a genuinely async backend or store — e.g. one that hits a remote IDP via httpx.AsyncClient — declare its methods async def and they are awaited directly without the thread hop:

class HttpxAuthBackend:
    async def authenticate(self, request):
        async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
            response = await client.get(
                "https://idp.example/userinfo",
                headers={"Authorization": request.META.get("HTTP_AUTHORIZATION", "")},
            )
        if response.status_code != 200:
            return None
        return TokenInfo(user=response.json()["sub"], scopes=())

    def protected_resource_metadata(self):
        return ProtectedResourceMetadata(resource="https://example.com/mcp/")

    def www_authenticate_challenge(self, *, scopes=None, error=None):
        return 'Bearer realm="mcp"'


server = MCPServer(name="my-app", auth_backend=HttpxAuthBackend())

The acall helper detects coroutine-functions at runtime via inspect.iscoroutinefunction and routes accordingly — no marker interface required.

The bridging runs one way only

Sync collaborators work under async_urls. An async collaborator does not work under the sync server.urls: that view has no event loop to await on, and an un-awaited coroutine is truthy, so an async authenticate mounted there would authenticate every caller. The sync transport refuses such a request with ImproperlyConfigured instead of serving it. Mount an async backend under async_urls only — see Write an async-native auth backend.

docs.title: Sync vs async services
docs.text:
Both work under async_urls:

  • Async services (async def create_invoice(*, data)) run native via arun_service. The full request handling stays on the event loop.
  • Sync services (def create_invoice(*, data)) are dispatched through sync_to_async. Django's connection pooling handles the thread hop correctly; ORM calls inside the service work without SynchronousOnlyOperation errors.

The same applies to selectors. Mix freely — the dispatch path picks the right strategy per call.

docs.title: Server-initiated push (SSE on GET)
docs.text:
When a session opens GET /mcp/, the async view returns a text/event-stream response. The server pushes JSON-RPC payloads on that stream as events; the client interprets each data: line as one MCP message. Idle periods produce SSE keep-alive comments (: keepalive) every ~15 seconds so reverse proxies don't close the connection.

# from app code (a service, a Django signal, a background task — anything
# running in the same process as the MCP server):
await server.notify(
    session_id,
    {
        "jsonrpc": "2.0",
        "method": "notifications/progress",
        "params": {"progressToken": "task-7", "value": 0.42},
    },
)

notify returns True if a subscriber was attached, False otherwise. A miss is normal — sessions without an open SSE stream just don't see the event. Most callers fire-and-forget.

docs.title: Wire details
docs.text:
The endpoint enforces the same headers as POST: Mcp-Protocol-Version required, Mcp-Session-Id required and validated against the session store. Origin allowlist applies. With no broker configured (e.g. a MCPServer(sse_broker=None)), GET returns 405 — spec-compliant when the server has nothing to push. So does SESSIONS_ENABLED = False, since a session id is what addresses a client's channel.

Either 405 is decided before authentication, so it is what an unauthenticated caller sees too. This is deliberate: no credential opens a stream that isn't on offer, and answering 401 there would hand the client a WWW-Authenticate challenge — the signal it uses to start an OAuth flow, and a browser window in desktop clients — for a token that changes nothing. Where a broker is wired and sessions are on, GET authenticates first as before.

docs.title: Scaling across workers
docs.text:
The default InMemorySSEBroker is single-process. A multi-worker deployment can:

  • Keep SSE on a single process by running one ASGI worker (or pinning SSE-enabled requests to one worker via session affinity). The simplest path and works for most apps.
  • Use the first-party RedisSSEBroker (behind the [redis] extra) — pass it as MCPServer(sse_broker=RedisSSEBroker(client)). See Multi-worker SSE with Redis.
  • Roll your own — implement subscribe / unsubscribe / publish against NATS, Kafka, etc., and pass it as MCPServer(sse_broker=...).

The single-subscriber rule applies per-session: re-subscribing replaces the previous queue. Message replay across reconnects is opt-in via an SSEReplayBuffer (InMemorySSEReplayBuffer or RedisSSEReplayBuffer) passed as MCPServer(sse_replay_buffer=...); with no buffer configured, Last-Event-ID is silently ignored. See SSE replay buffer.

docs.title: When sync is the right answer
docs.text: If you don't have async-native services and aren't running ASGI today, server.urls is the simpler path. Switching to async without genuine async work below the dispatch layer adds complexity (thread pool, connection management, more failure modes) without buying anything observable.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: django-spec-mcp is a resource server: it validates bearer tokens that someone else issued. The library does not implement a token issuer (that's the job of an Authorization Server / IDP), and it does not verify a token for you: how a token is verified depends on the authorization server a project runs, so that backend is the project's to write. What ships is the seam: the MCPAuthBackend protocol, the bearer_challenge helper that builds the 401 challenge, the exact audience comparison, the RFC 9728 metadata view clients use to discover your authorization server, and AllowAnyBackend for development.

docs.title: The pieces
docs.text:
Surface Protocol Default MCPAuthBackend Authenticate request → TokenInfo, build WWW-Authenticate, supply PRM payload none: auth_backend= is required to mount, and urls / async_urls refuse without one The spec's permissions Kernel PermissionChecks guarding a tool or resource required: a spec with none is refused at registration scopes= OAuth scopes a binding's caller must carry None (no scope gate) permissions= on a prompt or view Kernel PermissionChecks, each handed the binding as the spec None (no checks; [] is refused, as on a spec); a prompt with neither these nor scopes= is refused /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource RFC 9728 metadata served from backend's protected_resource_metadata()

The transport flow on every request:

  1. Validate Origin, MCP-Protocol-Version, MCP-Session-Id (where required).
  2. backend.authenticate(request) → TokenInfo | None. None, the answer for a caller the backend cannot authenticate, → 401 with the challenge from backend.www_authenticate_challenge(error=...): error="invalid_token" when the request sent an Authorization header, error=None when it sent none (RFC 6750 3.1: a request with no credentials gets no error code). A backend that raises instead is not answered as MCP: a PermissionDenied or Http404 renders as Django's own HTML 403 or 404, and anything else is a 500. From here on request.user and request.auser() are the token's principal.
  3. The binding's scope gate and its spec's permissions are asked; a denial → 403, with any required scopes surfaced in the challenge.
  4. Handler dispatched.

docs.title: AllowAnyBackend (dev only)
docs.text:
Authenticates every request as anonymous. The metadata payload is intentionally minimal and includes a _warning. Don't ship this to production.

Pass it when you build the server:

from django_spec_mcp import MCPServer
from django_spec_mcp.auth.backends.allow_any_backend import AllowAnyBackend

server = MCPServer(name="dev", auth_backend=AllowAnyBackend())

docs.title: Writing your own backend
docs.text:
A mounted server has no default backend. Every request to its endpoint reaches authenticate(), and a package default would either verify against an authorization server you may not run or answer every caller, so server.urls and server.async_urls raise ImproperlyConfigured when auth_backend= was not given. A server used purely in process (call_tool, list_tools) never authenticates and needs no backend.

A backend implements MCPAuthBackend:

Method Answers authenticate(request) A TokenInfo for a request carrying a valid token, None for one that does not (the transport answers 401) protected_resource_metadata() The RFC 9728 document served at .well-known/oauth-protected-resource: the resource's URL and the authorization servers that issue tokens for it www_authenticate_challenge(scopes=, error=) The WWW-Authenticate value of a 401 or an insufficient-scope 403. A 401 passes error="invalid_token" when the request sent an Authorization header and error=None when it did not; a 403 passes error="insufficient_scope" with the scopes

This one verifies tokens with a function the project supplies (a JWKS check, an introspection call, a database lookup) and binds each token to this server's URL:

from django.http import HttpRequest

from django_spec_mcp.auth import TokenInfo, bearer_challenge
from django_spec_mcp.auth.audience import audience_matches
from django_spec_mcp.auth.types.protected_resource_metadata import ProtectedResourceMetadata


class BearerBackend:
    """Verifies tokens an outside authorization server issued for this server."""

    def __init__(self, *, resource_url, authorization_server, scopes_supported, verify):
        self._resource_url = resource_url
        self._authorization_server = authorization_server
        self._scopes_supported = scopes_supported
        self._verify = verify  # raw token -> TokenInfo, or None when it does not verify

    def authenticate(self, request: HttpRequest) -> TokenInfo | None:
        scheme, _, raw = request.headers.get("Authorization", "").partition(" ")
        if scheme.lower() != "bearer" or not raw:
            return None
        info = self._verify(raw)
        # The audience MUST: a token issued for another resource on the same
        # authorization server verifies fine and must still be refused here.
        if info is None or not audience_matches(info.audience, self._resource_url):
            return None
        return info

    def protected_resource_metadata(self) -> ProtectedResourceMetadata:
        return ProtectedResourceMetadata(
            resource=self._resource_url,
            authorization_servers=[self._authorization_server],
            scopes_supported=list(self._scopes_supported),
        )

    def www_authenticate_challenge(self, *, scopes=None, error=None) -> str:
        # The server mounts its metadata view under its own URL, so the pointer
        # a client follows to find the authorization server is derived from it.
        return bearer_challenge(
            resource_metadata_url=(
                f"{self._resource_url.rstrip('/')}/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource"
            ),
            scopes=scopes,
            error=error,
        )

from django_spec_mcp import MCPServer

server = MCPServer(
    name="internal-mcp",
    auth_backend=BearerBackend(
        resource_url="https://example.com/internal/mcp/",
        authorization_server="https://idp.example.com",
        scopes_supported=["invoices:read", "invoices:write"],
        verify=verify_access_token,
    ),
)

bearer_challenge(resource_metadata_url=, scopes=, error=) is where the header is formatted, once: the realm, then resource_metadata, error and scope in the order a client reads them. resource_metadata_url has no default on purpose. It is the URL a client follows to find your authorization server, and a challenge without it leaves the client no way to start the flow, with no error on either side. Pass the URL the server's protected-resource-metadata route answers at (https://example.com/internal/mcp/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource for a server whose resource URL is https://example.com/internal/mcp/), or None when the backend publishes no metadata.

Mounting is where a backend becomes load-bearing, so a backend may check itself there: one that implements check_configuration() (the SelfChecking protocol) is asked once when server.urls or server.async_urls is read, and raising ImproperlyConfigured from it surfaces while the URLconf is imported, which manage.py check reaches, rather than as a 500 on the first request. A backend that needs no setup implements nothing and is left alone.

name and version belong on the server

SERVER_INFO["name"] / ["version"] are the fallback for a server built without name= / version=. Prefer the constructor — it is the only way to give two servers in one project distinct identities:

MCPServer(name="internal", version="2.0.0", url_namespace="internal-mcp")

docs.title: Who may call a tool
docs.text:
A tool or resource is guarded by its spec's permissions: a list of kernel PermissionCheck instances, the same checks every other transport on the kernel asks. Each is asked through the kernel's dispatch of the principal the backend resolved, TokenInfo.user, before any rate limit is charged, the target is looked up or the service runs.

Registering a spec that declares no permissions at all is refused: ImproperlyConfigured at registration. [Unrestricted()] is the honest choice for an operation open to every caller, because it says so out loud. Set SPEC_MCP["REQUIRE_TOOL_PERMISSIONS"] = False to downgrade the refusal to an UnguardedToolWarning; a spec declaring permissions=None then runs each call under a kernel Grant built for that spec and that caller, so it is called with no permission check. A scopes= gate does not count as a guard either way. See Kernel specs.

A check is a subclass with a has_permission(principal, spec) method. A Django permission is a few lines:

from django_service_specs import PermissionCheck, ServiceSpec


class HasDjangoPerm(PermissionCheck):
    def __init__(self, codename: str) -> None:
        self.codename = codename

    def has_permission(self, principal, spec) -> bool:
        return principal.has_perm(self.codename)


server.register_tool(
    ServiceSpec(service=refund_invoice, permissions=[HasDjangoPerm("invoices.refund_invoice")]),
    name="invoices.refund",
    description="Refund an invoice.",
    scopes=("invoices:write",),
)

A check refusing the caller is answered -32006 "Insufficient permission" with HTTP 403. The challenge names no scope, because no scope the client could obtain would change the answer.

A check that depends on the token rather than the user, a claim say, asks for the call's context by declaring a keyword call_context. Over HTTP its "request" is the Django HttpRequest, carrying the backend's TokenInfo as request.mcp_token; request.user and request.auser() are the token's principal from authentication on, whatever the session cookie names. An in-process call_tool or acall_tool is not over HTTP: its "request" may be None, or a request whose mcp_token, when it has one, carries the scopes= the call passed and raw=None. So a check reading the token decides for itself what an in-process call means, and never tells one apart by request is None:

from django_service_specs import PermissionCheck


class HasClaim(PermissionCheck):
    def __init__(self, claim: str) -> None:
        self.claim = claim

    def has_permission(self, principal, spec, *, call_context) -> bool:
        request = call_context.get("request")
        token = getattr(request, "mcp_token", None)
        return token is not None and self.claim in (token.raw or {})

A check may ask for the call's arguments the same way, and for a registered pool seed by its name. A check is synchronous: one declaring an async def method is refused with ImproperlyConfigured when the spec is built, because an un-awaited coroutine is truthy and would allow every call.

docs.title: The scope gate
docs.text:
scopes= on register_tool, register_resource, register_prompt and register_ui_resource names the OAuth scopes the caller's token must carry, every one of them. A bare string is one scope: scopes="invoices:write". A token missing one is answered -32006 with HTTP 403, every declared scope in data.requiredScopes, and a challenge carrying error="insufficient_scope" and the scopes, so the client knows what to ask for. scopes=() is refused, since it would read as a gate and admit every caller.

The scope gate is a transport check, beside the spec's permissions rather than in place of them: on a tool or resource it never satisfies REQUIRE_TOOL_PERMISSIONS, which reads the spec's own permissions. A prompt has no spec, so there either guard counts.

docs.title: Prompts and interactive views
docs.text:
A prompt and an interactive view are not specs, so they are gated where they are registered: register_prompt and register_ui_resource take permissions=[...], a list of the same kernel PermissionChecks a spec declares, and scopes=, the scope gate above. The scope gate is asked first, then a deactivated caller is refused, then each check in order, the first refusal ending it. A check is asked has_permission(principal, binding): principal is the token's user, an AnonymousUser when it has none, and binding is the prompt's or view's binding standing where a spec would, so a check can read its name.

from django_service_specs import PermissionCheck


class IsStaff(PermissionCheck):
    message = "Staff only."

    def has_permission(self, principal, spec) -> bool:
        return bool(principal.is_staff)


server.register_prompt(
    name="summarise-ledger",
    render=render_summary,
    permissions=[IsStaff()],
    scopes="ledger:read",
)

The same judgement answers prompts/get, resources/read, completion/complete and a subscription. With FILTER_LISTINGS_BY_PERMISSIONS on, it answers prompts/list and resources/list too, so a caller is never shown a prompt or view it would then be refused; with the setting off, the default, the listings show every prompt and view. In a filtered listing a check that raises hides its own prompt or view and no other, as a spec's check that cannot decide without a call's arguments hides only its tool; an ImproperlyConfigured still fails the listing, as it fails the call.

Registration holds the list to the kernel's rule for a spec's permissions, through the kernel's own check_permissions: a bare string or anything else that is not a sequence, a check class rather than an instance, an object that is not a PermissionCheck, a check with an async def method, whose answer would be a truthy coroutine nothing awaits, and an empty list, which reads as a gate and admits everyone, are each refused. Leave permissions= out for no checks, or declare [Unrestricted()]. A check that answers a coroutine anyway at call time is refused there by the kernel's sync_answer. Only the principal and the binding are passed: the keywords a spec's check may opt into, such as arguments or call_context, are the kernel's to offer at dispatch, so a check that requires one cannot gate a prompt.

A prompt with neither permissions= nor scopes= is refused like a tool. Interactive views (register_ui_resource) are the one exemption, and a deliberate one — a view is a template rendered with no context, a literal document, or a zero-argument callable, none of which can read the caller's data.

That third source is caller-blind because registration enforces it: a render= declaring any fillable parameter is refused, since the read path resolves every binding's callable against a pool carrying request and user. Without that refusal the exemption would be unsound for one of its three cases — a caller-aware view registered unguarded, served into a document hosts may cache across callers. If you want a view whose content depends on who is asking, you want register_resource, where the declaration check applies.

docs.title: Object-level permissions
docs.text:
A check's has_object_permission(principal, spec, target) runs against the row the dispatch resolved: the target of a retrieve, or the instance an update acts on. It allows by default, because most checks are class-level only. has_scope_permission(principal, spec, scope) is the same question for a call that resolves no single row: the set a bulk call acts on or a collection reads, and None for a create. A kernel spec's checks are asked once on a plain call, and on a streamed call once in its pre-flight and once more when the call runs, when its arguments pass the kernel's argument check.

A resource read runs the same dispatch, so its spec's checks see the row the URI names. completion/complete on a resource template names the template rather than a URI, so the spec's checks are asked on no arguments, and a check scoping by a URI variable refuses the completion, whether it answers no on the missing arguments or raises on them.

docs.title: Filtering listings by permissions
docs.text:
By default tools/list, resources/list, resources/templates/list, and prompts/list return every registered binding regardless of whether the current caller's permissions would let it invoke one. (A tool that an operation-scope affordance refuses right now is the exception: tools/list leaves it out either way, because that condition cannot depend on the call's arguments — see Concepts.) Set SPEC_MCP["FILTER_LISTINGS_BY_PERMISSIONS"] = True to drop bindings whose permissions deny the caller before paginating.

This is binding-level gating. A binding's scopes= gate is evaluated against the caller's token, and a prompt's or view's checks against its principal, as a prompts/get or resources/read asks them. A tool or resource is judged by its spec's own checks as well, asked through the kernel's authorize with no arguments, because a listing has none; a create, a service spec with no instance or collection selector, is also asked each check's has_scope_permission of None, as every call to it is. Both questions get the caller's principal, the server's pool seeds and a call_context whose request carries the token, as a call does. A caller the checks refuse is not shown the binding, and neither is a deactivated caller. A spec declaring permissions=None is listed only where its call is granted, as register_tool grants it with REQUIRE_TOOL_PERMISSIONS off.

A spec's check whose decision depends on the call arguments cannot answer at list time and will conservatively deny: when asking it raises, that binding alone is hidden and the rest of the listing is unaffected. Mark such a binding with always_listed=True to keep it visible as a discovery aid; the check still gates the actual invocation. An ImproperlyConfigured raised by a check is not a refusal: it is raised and fails the listing, because the call raises it too.

docs.title: Audience binding (RFC 8707)
docs.text:
The audience check is the backend's job, because only the backend knows where the audience lives (a JWT aud claim, an introspection response, a column on the token row). TokenInfo.audience carries it out, and audience_matches is the comparison, as the worked backend above calls it:

  • audience_matches(token_audience, expected) is exact equality. Token audiences are URLs, not patterns, and a prefix or substring match is unsafe: a token bound to …/mcp would otherwise satisfy a server expecting …/mcp-admin.
  • A token that carries no audience is rejected when an expected URL is given, which is the point of configuring one.
  • expected=None disables the check, for a deployment whose gateway already binds the token upstream.

The MCP spec makes this a MUST

2026-07-28 says a resource server MUST validate that access tokens were issued specifically for it. A backend that only verifies a signature leaves a conformance gap, and the failure mode is cross-resource token replay: a token minted for a different resource on the same authorization server is accepted here. Before you require it, check that the clients you serve send RFC 8707's resource parameter on the authorize and token requests, because a token that carries none is rejected.

Each server needs its own canonical URL. RFC 8707 binds a token to a resource, and that binding is what stops a token issued for one resource being replayed against another; two servers sharing one URL defeat it:

# urls.py
common = {
    "authorization_server": "https://idp.example.com",
    "scopes_supported": ["invoices:read"],
    "verify": verify_access_token,
}
internal = MCPServer(
    name="internal-mcp",
    auth_backend=BearerBackend(resource_url="https://example.com/internal/mcp/", **common),
    url_namespace="internal-mcp",
)
public = MCPServer(
    name="public-mcp",
    auth_backend=BearerBackend(resource_url="https://example.com/public/mcp/", **common),
    url_namespace="public-mcp",
)

urlpatterns = [
    path("internal/mcp/", internal.urls),
    path("public/mcp/", public.urls),
]

A token minted for public-mcp is now rejected by internal-mcp, and each server's WWW-Authenticate challenge points at its own metadata endpoint.

docs.title: If you are writing a resource server against the official mcp SDK
docs.text:
The SDK publishes the metadata for you and never validates the audience

This is the single easiest thing to get wrong in this area, and it is not specific to this package — it is worth knowing wherever you build an MCP resource server in Python.

mcp.shared.auth_utils provides resource_url_from_server_url() and check_resource_allowed(), and in the shipped wheel they are called only from client paths. AccessToken carries a resource field, but BearerAuthBackend.authenticate() checks the bearer prefix, the verifier's verdict and expires_at — and nothing else.

So a TokenVerifier that merely checks a signature is non-compliant with the audience MUST, and cross-resource token replay works: a token minted for another resource on the same authorization server is accepted. FastMCP's JWTVerifier does validate audience out of the box; the official SDK's verifiers do not. If you are writing your own verifier anywhere, validate the audience in it.

docs.title: Try it with mcp-inspector
docs.text:
npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --url http://localhost:8000/mcp/

Inspector reads the protected-resource metadata, hits your authorization server's metadata, walks the auth flow, and exercises tools/list + tools/call. Common failure modes and where to look:

Symptom Likely cause 401 with no WWW-Authenticate The backend's www_authenticate_challenge returned an empty value. Return bearer_challenge(...). 401 with WWW-Authenticate but no resource_metadata The backend passed resource_metadata_url=None to bearer_challenge. Token verifies but every call is still 401 The backend's audience comparison fails: the token's audience is not the server's own resource URL (or the token carries none). 403 with error="insufficient_scope" and scope= in the challenge Token authenticated, missing one of the per-binding scopes. The body also carries JSON-RPC -32006 with data.requiredScopes. 403 with no scope= A spec's permission check refused the caller, or a prompt's or view's own check. RFC 6750 defines no error code for that case, so the challenge advertises nothing rather than a scope the client cannot obtain. 403 with INVALID_REQUEST (-32600) in the body Not a permission failure — Origin rejection.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: A short tour of every moving part. Read this once; the rest of the docs assume you have these in your head.

docs.title: A kernel spec is the unit of registration
docs.text:
The MCP server does not wrap, walk, or otherwise reach into views or routers. It serves django_service_specs specs: a ServiceSpec for an operation that writes, a SelectorSpec for one that reads. The spec is the whole declaration of the operation (what it takes, who may run it, how its result is presented), so the same spec serves every transport built on the kernel, and a project needs no view at all to expose it over MCP.

MCPServer.register_tool takes a spec positionally. The spec's class decides the kind of tool: a ServiceSpec is a service tool, a SelectorSpec a selector tool. register_resource takes a RETRIEVE SelectorSpec the same way.

from django_service_specs import (
    DataclassPresenter,
    DataclassValidator,
    Parameter,
    Parameters,
    SelectorKind,
    SelectorSpec,
    ServiceSpec,
    Unrestricted,
)

server.register_tool(
    ServiceSpec(
        service=record_invoice,
        validator=DataclassValidator(InvoiceInput),
        presenter=DataclassPresenter(InvoiceOutput),
        permissions=[Unrestricted()],
    ),
    name="invoices.create",
    description="Create an invoice.",
)
server.register_tool(
    SelectorSpec(
        kind=SelectorKind.LIST,
        selector=list_invoices,
        presenter=DataclassPresenter(InvoiceOutput),
        permissions=[Unrestricted()],
    ),
    name="invoices.list",
    description="List invoices.",
    paginate=True,
)
server.register_resource(
    SelectorSpec(
        kind=SelectorKind.RETRIEVE,
        selector=invoice_by_pk,
        reads=Parameters([Parameter("pk", "integer", required=True)]),
        presenter=DataclassPresenter(InvoiceOutput),
        permissions=[Unrestricted()],
    ),
    name="invoice",
    uri_template="invoices://{pk}",
)

Anything that is not a kernel spec is refused with a TypeError at registration.

docs.title: What a spec carries through to MCP
docs.text:
Every field a spec declares is the kernel's to run, so it means on this transport what it means on any other:

  • permissions are kernel PermissionChecks, and they are the spec's guard. The call asks them of the principal the auth backend resolved for the request. An operation open to every caller declares [Unrestricted()].
  • reads are the arguments the callable takes, as kernel Parameters; shapes are the read-shaping values its presenter reads (Read-shaping values). Both are advertised in the tool's inputSchema, and a Parameter's help is its property's description.
  • validator checks a service's input. Its fields are the tool's arguments, spread at the top level of arguments as the kernel's spec_input_schema advertises them, with no data key around them. A many=True service takes a list instead (A list payload).
  • presenter renders the result, and its output schema, through the kernel's spec_output_schema, is the tool's outputSchema.
  • kind is the required SelectorKind, LIST or RETRIEVE. It decides whether the tool serves a list or one object, and which knobs the registration accepts: a RETRIEVE takes no paginate=.
  • Queryset shaping (select_related, prefetch_related, annotations, extend_queryset, filter_set), the target lookups (instance_selector_spec, collection_selector_spec), the output re-read (output_selector_spec), preconditions, affordances, atomic and allow_none all run inside the kernel's dispatch.
  • kwargs= is a per-spec provider of extra keyword arguments, called through the keyword pool, so it declares the entries it needs by name (user, the call's request, a registered seed). A key a provider whose return annotation is a TypedDict always fills is the server's, and is left out of the inputSchema.
  • idempotent reaches the tool's annotations (Tool annotations).

docs.title: How a tool is called
docs.text:
• The call is the kernel's dispatch / adispatch. The principal is the token's user, an AnonymousUser for a token naming no one and for call_tool(..., user=None). The call context holds request, view (always None here), format and action, the tool's name. Over HTTP, call_context["request"] is the transport's Django HttpRequest, with the resolved token as request.mcp_token and the token's principal as request.user. An in-process call has no HTTP request of its own: acall_tool puts a token built from its user= on the request it works on, and sync call_tool puts none there, even when the request handed to it carried one, so a check reading request.mcp_token finds nothing under call_tool (Transport-neutral invocation).
  • The spec's own permissions answer the call, before the rate limit is charged. A refused principal is -32006 "Insufficient permission", uncharged, and call_tool, which charges nothing, raises the kernel's NotPermitted before it checks the arguments. A check declaring arguments is shown them as the kernel's argument check reads them, so "8" sent for an integer reaches it as 8, and a URI's true for a boolean as True. The checks are asked once per call whose arguments pass that check, twice when the call streams progress (only the async transport streams). A call whose arguments fail that check is never shown them: it is judged as a filtered listing judges the spec, its checks asked on no arguments, and is refused -32006 before the charge when they refuse; otherwise a tool call is told which argument is wrong after the charge. A many call whose top level passes and whose rows do not is the exception: its checks answer on the checked top level, a refusal as -32006 before the charge, and an admitted caller is told the rows after it. A resource's completion has no arguments and is judged the same way. A tool registered with a task_policy= other than the default has the checks asked before its task is created, and again by the task's worker (Opting a tool in).
  • The schemas are the kernel's spec_input_schema / spec_output_schema. unknown_arguments= reaches both the schema and the call, and server_arguments= names are left out of the schema and filled by the server.
  • A declaration no call could run is refused at registration. register_tool, register_tools and register_resource ask the kernel's check_seeds with the server's pool_seeds= and raise ImproperlyConfigured, naming the tool or resource, for a parameter named like a registered seed or the call's own request or view, a positional-only parameter with no default, a keyword the callable requires that nothing fills, and an optional read over a keyword the callable requires. A read always sent is checked as required and registers: one the tool's server_arguments= binds a value to, and one a resource's URI template names, which the matcher fills on every read. An optional read neither covers is still refused.
  • scopes= is the transport's gate. A token must carry every scope named; one that is missing any is answered -32006 with every declared scope in requiredScopes, not only the missing ones. A bare string is one scope. scopes=() is refused, since it reads as a gate and admits everyone. A KernelToolBinding or KernelResourceBinding built by hand and passed to server.tools.register or server.resources.register derives the same gate from its own scopes and refuses () the same way.
  • A spec declaring permissions=None is unguarded. With REQUIRE_TOOL_PERMISSIONS on, the default, registering one is refused. With it off, the tool or resource registers with one UnguardedToolWarning and every call runs without a permission check, under a kernel Grant minted for that spec and the calling principal. A spec with permissions of its own is never granted: its checks run whatever the setting says. Only register_tool and register_resource grant; a kernel SpecRegistry refuses such a spec when it is built, so register_tools never receives one. A KernelToolBinding or KernelResourceBinding built by hand and passed to server.tools.register or server.resources.register is never granted, whatever the setting, so the kernel refuses its unguarded spec at the call and the operation does not run. An operation open to every caller declares [Unrestricted()] instead. The scope gate does not count as a guard.
  • Registration refuses what a tool cannot mean: paginate= / max_page_size= on a service tool or a RETRIEVE, invalidates= on a selector tool, and UnknownArguments.PASSTHROUGH. task_policy= is taken by either kind of tool, as Opting a tool in describes.

docs.title: Project-wide seeds: pool_seeds=
docs.text:
A spec's kwargs= provider is per spec. What every spec on a mount may read — a tenant, a locale, a clock — is a seed, registered once on the server as a kernel PoolSeeds, the same registry the kernel's dispatch(pool_seeds=) takes:

from django_service_specs import DEFAULT_POOL_SEEDS


def tenant_of(*, user):
    # An anonymous caller has no tenant, and resolves to none rather than raising.
    return getattr(user, "tenant", None)


server = MCPServer(
    name="billing",
    pool_seeds=DEFAULT_POOL_SEEDS.extend(tenant=tenant_of),
)


def list_invoices(*, tenant):  # receives the resolved tenant on every call
    return Invoice.objects.filter(tenant=tenant)

A resolver is called through the keyword pool like every other provider, so it declares the entries it needs (user, request) and is resolved per call against the caller. The default is the kernel's own DEFAULT_POOL_SEEDS, which registers nothing, so a server that passes none adds nothing to the pool.

A resolver must answer for every caller the mount admits, an anonymous one included whenever the auth backend lets one through, because the listing reads it too. Once any tool declares an operation condition, tools/list resolves the seeds for its caller (see the second bullet below), so a resolver that raises for a caller fails that caller's whole listing, not only its calls. lambda *, user: user.tenant is the form that does: an AnonymousUser has no tenant.

  • Every spec the server runs receives them. A service or selector tool over either transport and either era, call_tool / acall_tool, a task the worker runs, and a resource's spec on resources/read.
  • The availability check asks with them too. tools/list, list_tools and unavailable_tools resolve the seeds into the pool they ask an operation condition against, so when=lambda *, tenant: tenant.can_close_books is asked the same question at the listing as at the call (A tool that cannot run now is not listed).
  • A registered name is never the caller's. It is left out of the tool's inputSchema and never required, and a caller sending it anyway is answered as for any argument the spec does not declare: refused under UnknownArguments.REJECT, dropped under IGNORE. The seed's value is the only one the callable receives.
  • Registration agrees with dispatch. A callable declaring a seed with no default registers, since the seed is always supplied. A read named after a seed, and a URI-template variable named after one, are refused, since the argument and the seed would meet in one pool.
  • One set per mount, with no per-call or per-tool override. What varies per call belongs in the resolver; a mount needing different seeds is a second MCPServer.

Prompt rendering and argument completion call bare callables rather than specs, and do not receive the seeds.

docs.title: Which parameters a client is asked for
docs.text:
A tool advertises its spec's parameters: the reads, the shapes, a service's validator fields, and a target lookup's reads. The kernel lists every parameter as declared, required meaning the call needs the value from someone, and the server leaves out of the schema what it answers itself:

  • a name the server fills whatever the caller sends is left out of properties and required: the tool's server_arguments, a registered seed, and a key a typed kwargs= or input_data= provider always fills (the kernel's server_owned_keys);
  • a parameter a provider may fill is offered and not required, because dispatch does not demand it of the caller (the kernel's provider_reached). A key whose TypedDict value admits UnsetType is one the provider may decline, and a provider whose return is not a TypedDict, a plain -> dict or a lambda included, may fill any parameter, so beside one nothing it reaches is required. Annotate the provider to have the rest inferred.
from typing_extensions import TypedDict

from django_service_specs import Parameter, Parameters, SelectorKind, SelectorSpec


class Scope(TypedDict):
    tenant: str


def scope(*, request) -> Scope:  # annotated, so `tenant` is known to be filled
    return {"tenant": request.user.tenant}


spec = SelectorSpec(
    kind=SelectorKind.RETRIEVE,
    selector=get_invoice,  # def get_invoice(*, pk: int, tenant: str)
    reads=Parameters([Parameter("pk", "integer", required=True)]),
    kwargs=scope,
    permissions=[IsBillingStaff()],
)  # inputSchema: {"pk"}, required ["pk"]

A call that leaves out a required argument is refused before the callable runs, with a validation_error result naming what is missing, keyed in detail by the missing name, on every route (both transports and eras, call_tool and acall_tool):

{"error": {"type": "validation_error", "message": "Missing required argument(s): `pk`.",
           "detail": {"pk": ["This field is required."]}}}

The message is the server's conventions.missing_arguments, worded with every name the kernel's InvalidArguments.missing carries, sorted and in backticks, and the detail is the kernel's per-field detail. A call that left one argument out and sent another wrong names the missing one in the message and both in the detail; a refusal naming nothing missing answers "Invalid arguments".

The check runs after the permission answer: a caller the spec's checks refuse is refused for the permission first, and never learns from a missing-argument answer that the tool exists. An admitted caller is told about the argument after the rate limit is charged.

docs.title: Read-shaping values: shapes
docs.text:
A spec's shapes are the caller's values its presenter reads while it renders the result: a field selection, an expansion flag. They are Parameters like reads, advertised in the tool's inputSchema beside them, and the presenter receives them on its PresentationContext.shapes:

from django_service_specs import Parameter, Parameters, SelectorKind, SelectorSpec

server.register_tool(
    SelectorSpec(
        kind=SelectorKind.LIST,
        selector=list_invoices,
        shapes=Parameters(
            [Parameter("fields", "array", items="string", help="Fields to return, e.g. id, number")]
        ),
        presenter=FieldSelectingPresenter(InvoiceOutput),
        permissions=[IsBillingStaff()],
    ),
    name="invoices.list",
    description="List invoices.",
    paginate=True,
)

docs.title: On a paged tool it shapes each item, never the page
docs.text:
With paginate=True the tool serves the {items, page, totalPages, hasNext} envelope, and the presenter never sees it: the envelope is built around the rows the presenter rendered, so a shape reaches only a row. A selection therefore names the fields of one item, never the envelope's: ["id", "number"] rather than ["items"]. That is the easy mistake to make, because the outputSchema a model reads describes the envelope. So on a paged tool, each shape's description in the inputSchema ends with:

On a paged result it applies to each item in items, never to the page envelope (items, page, totalPages, hasNext).

A service tool and an unpaginated list have no envelope, and get no sentence. The words are the server's conventions.query_param_on_pages, which can change them or drop them; whether the sentence appears stays the server's call.

The package does not rewrite a selection written the other way: a shape is opaque to the transport, so correcting one would mean knowing every grammar a presenter might parse. What it controls is what the caller hears when the presenter refuses a value, and that depends on how the presenter selects:

  • Strict selection, a presenter that raises the kernel's ServiceValidationError for a name it does not know. That comes back as an isError: true tool result of type validation_error, the same shape a service's ServiceValidationError produces (Dispatch flow), and its message names the argument, then gives the presenter's own words: "fields was rejected while rendering the result: Unknown field items." The transport adds nothing about any one grammar. On a paged tool the per-item sentence follows it. The detail is keyed under the shape's name; when a call supplied several shapes it sits under non_field_errors and the message names them all, because nothing says which one the presenter refused. A model reads the result and retries with a corrected selection.
  • Tolerant selection, a presenter that drops the names it does not know, answers ["items"] with a page of {}: one empty object per row, a well-formed result no transport can tell from a real one. It opts out of the error signal entirely, so tools an agent calls should select strictly — that is the setting in which the model can correct itself.

The tool result is reserved for the failures the caller caused. A presenter's ServiceValidationError becomes one only when the call sent a non-null value for at least one of the spec's shapes. A shape the tool's server_arguments binds does not count, because a value the server supplied is not the caller's to correct, and neither does a null. With nothing sent the presenter refused on its own, no retry could change the outcome, and it stays a server error — over HTTP a JSON-RPC -32603 reading Internal error under a 500, with the exception in the log; from call_tool and acall_tool, the exception itself. Anything else a presenter raises is a server error whatever the caller sent: an AttributeError in a presenter is a bug, not a bad argument. Every path a tool is presented on answers alike: both transports, sync and async, and the in-process call_tool.

A resource whose URI template names a shape answers the same refusal of a value its URI carried as the read answers a bad URI variable: JSON-RPC -32602 "Invalid arguments", with the detail keyed by the shape under data.detail, or under non_field_errors when the URI carried several. With no shape in the URI it is the internal error.

docs.title: Server-supplied arguments: server_arguments=
docs.text:
When the mount already knows an argument - a server scoped to one project, a deployment that always reads one tenant - asking the model for it is both wasted tokens and a door left open: the model can send another project's id. server_arguments= answers the argument for the caller instead. It takes a ServerArguments from django_service_specs, on register_tool and as a register_tools override, and each route checks it the same way:

from django_service_specs import ServerArguments

server.register_tool(
    vendors_spec,  # reads: project_pk, draw_request_pk
    name="list_document_vendors",
    description="List the vendors on a project's documents.",
    server_arguments=ServerArguments(
        values={"project_pk": 7},  # this server's project, always
        withheld={"draw_request_pk"},  # never the caller's; the default applies
    ),
)
  • The names leave the tool's inputSchema and its required list, on tools/list and wherever else the schema is built, so the model is never asked for them. A bound value can fill a read the spec marks required=True.
  • A caller's value for one is dropped before anything reads it: the spec's permission checks, the missing-argument check and the callable all see the server's value. A value an elicitation answer carries is dropped the same way. The server logs the tool's name and the dropped argument names at WARNING, never the values; a caller restating the bound value is not logged. A withheld name is absent, so the callable runs on its own default.
  • It is checked at registration. A name the spec does not declare, a value its declared type refuses, a name the server fills as a pool seed, and a withheld name the callable cannot do without each raise ImproperlyConfigured naming the tool. A binding built by hand and passed to server.tools.register is checked there too.

The values are static for the life of the binding. A value computed per request - the project the signed-in user belongs to - is not something server_arguments carries: compute it in a kwargs= provider, or refuse the call in a permission check.

docs.title: A list payload: many=True service tools
docs.text:
A ServiceSpec with many=True validates its input as a list, item by item through its validator, and hands the service that list as data. A tools/call's arguments is always a JSON object, so here the list travels under one argument, named by the spec's many_argument, items unless the spec says otherwise:

from django_service_specs import DataclassValidator, ServiceSpec


def create_invoices(*, data):
    return [create_invoice(item) for item in data]


server.register_tool(
    ServiceSpec(
        service=create_invoices,
        validator=DataclassValidator(InvoiceInput),  # describes one item
        many=True,
        many_argument="invoices",  # optional; the default is "items"
        permissions=[IsBillingStaff()],
    ),
    name="invoices.bulk_create",
    description="Create several invoices at once.",
)

The tool advertises the argument as an array of the item schema, bounded by the maxItems the kernel's schema declares:

{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "invoices": {"type": "array", "maxItems": 1000,
                 "items": {"type": "object", "properties": {"number": {"type": "string"}}}}
  },
  "required": ["invoices"],
  "additionalProperties": false
}

What a caller should know:

  • The tool's unknown_arguments decides what travels beside the list. Under REJECT, the default, any other argument is refused and the top level of the schema is closed; under IGNORE it is dropped and the top level is open.
  • unknown_arguments applies inside each item too. Each item is checked as a single-item tool's arguments are, and each item's own additionalProperties says whether an undeclared key in it is refused.
  • Errors are keyed under the argument, and item errors by index. An invalid second item is a validation_error result whose error.detail is {"invoices": {"1": {"amount": ["Expected an integer."]}}}. JSON object keys are strings, so the index arrives as "1"; with INCLUDE_VALIDATION_VALUE on, error.value["invoices"][1] is the item it names. A call with no list is refused under the argument as missing.
  • The result is the service's list. It is presented as a list, and the outputSchema is an array of the item schema. structuredContent is that bare array, as for every unpaginated list result this server returns, not an object wrapping it.

docs.title: A resource is a RETRIEVE selector
docs.text:
register_resource(spec, *, uri_template, name, ...) takes a kernel SelectorSpec of kind RETRIEVE positionally, as register_tool does. The read runs the spec through the kernel's dispatch / adispatch, with the URI-template variables as its arguments, so the spec's reads name them and its presenter renders the row:

from django_service_specs import (
    DataclassPresenter,
    Parameter,
    Parameters,
    SelectorKind,
    SelectorSpec,
)

server.register_resource(
    SelectorSpec(
        kind=SelectorKind.RETRIEVE,
        selector=get_invoice,  # def get_invoice(*, pk): ...
        reads=Parameters([Parameter("pk", "integer", required=True)]),
        presenter=DataclassPresenter(InvoiceOutput),
        permissions=[IsBillingStaff()],
    ),
    name="invoice",
    uri_template="invoices://{pk}",
    description="One invoice, by primary key.",
)
  • A reader the spec's checks refuse is answered -32006 and is not charged. A reader they admit is charged, and a URI variable that fails the spec's argument check is then answered -32602 with message Invalid arguments and the kernel's detail tree under data.detail, as an admitted tool call is told which argument is wrong; INCLUDE_VALIDATION_VALUE adds the variables sent under data.value. scopes= gates a read as it gates a tool.
  • A uri_template variable must be a read or shape of the spec that the server does not fill. Registration raises ImproperlyConfigured naming the resource and the variable when no read or shape declares it, when the read seeds the name itself (the call's request, or a seed the server registers), and when a reflected read the server fills or a key a typed kwargs= provider always fills makes it the server's, since every read would be refused or would serve the server's value for any URI.

docs.title: What a resource carries, and what registration refuses
docs.text:
The read dispatches the spec itself, so everything it declares runs on a read as on a tool call: its permissions, its queryset shaping and its allow_none alike. What a resource cannot take is a shape the read has no room for, and registration refuses each one rather than serving something other than what was declared:

Refused Why A LIST spec A resource reads one row by URI. Register a LIST as a selector tool, which paginates. encoding=TEXT or BLOB beside a spec declaring affordances or allow_none The kernel adds affordances to a presented object, and under allow_none a missing row presents as None without the presenter running; neither is a document or bytes. Serve either as JSON. permissions= register_resource takes no such keyword, so passing one is a TypeError: the spec's own permissions are the resource's guard. A URI variable no read or shape declares, or one the server fills See above: every read would be refused, or would serve the server's value for any URI.

docs.title: The body a read serves
docs.text:
The read dispatches the spec, and its presenter renders the body: what the presenter's present returns is what encoding= turns into the contents entry. A spec with no presenter serves its selector's value the same way. mime_type= is advertised as given, on the read and in both listings, and is never inferred from the encoding or checked against the body:

encoding= The presenter returns Served as ResourceEncoding.JSON, the default anything JSON-encodable text, the value as JSON ResourceEncoding.TEXT a str: Markdown, CSV, HTML, plain text text, the string as written ResourceEncoding.BLOB bytes, bytearray or memoryview, a strided memoryview included blob, base64, and no text

A TEXT resource whose presenter renders the row as Markdown:

from django_service_specs import (
    Output,
    Parameter,
    Parameters,
    Presenter,
    SelectorKind,
    SelectorSpec,
)

from django_spec_mcp import ResourceEncoding


class InvoiceMarkdown(Presenter):
    def output(self) -> Output:
        return Output()  # a document, not an object of fields

    def present(self, value):
        return f"# Invoice {value.number}\n\nTotal: {value.total}"


server.register_resource(
    SelectorSpec(
        kind=SelectorKind.RETRIEVE,
        selector=get_invoice,
        reads=Parameters([Parameter("pk", "integer", required=True)]),
        presenter=InvoiceMarkdown(),
        permissions=[IsBillingStaff()],
    ),
    name="invoice-summary",
    uri_template="invoices://{pk}/summary",
    mime_type="text/markdown",
    encoding=ResourceEncoding.TEXT,
)

A BLOB resource whose presenter renders the same row as a PDF:

class InvoicePdf(Presenter):
    def output(self) -> Output:
        return Output()  # bytes, not an object of fields

    def present(self, value):
        return render_invoice_pdf(value)  # -> bytes


server.register_resource(
    SelectorSpec(
        kind=SelectorKind.RETRIEVE,
        selector=get_invoice,
        reads=Parameters([Parameter("pk", "integer", required=True)]),
        presenter=InvoicePdf(),
        permissions=[IsBillingStaff()],
    ),
    name="invoice-pdf",
    uri_template="invoices://{pk}/pdf",
    mime_type="application/pdf",
    encoding=ResourceEncoding.BLOB,
)
# resources/read of invoices://7/pdf answers a contents entry of
# {"uri": "invoices://7/pdf", "mimeType": "application/pdf", "blob": "JVBERi0..."}

A TEXT resource left at the default application/json is still served verbatim, since the mime type is never checked against the body.

A presenter returning the wrong type for its encoding is -32603. A dict under TEXT, or a str under BLOB, can only be found out by a read, so the read answers a JSON-RPC error with code -32603 rather than failing with a 500. The message names the resource, its encoding and the type it got, and sends the reader to the code that produced it:

Resource 'invoice-pdf' declares encoding=BLOB but produced str, not bytes. A BLOB
resource's body is the binary itself, base64-encoded here, so the spec's
presenter (or its selector, when it declares none) must return the bytes.

The result ceiling and the cache hints apply to every encoding alike. An HTML view the host renders is register_ui_resource, which sets both.

docs.title: Registering a whole SpecRegistry
docs.text:
register_tools(registry, *, overrides=None) registers every entry of a kernel SpecRegistry, in order, each under its registry name, with the knobs overrides holds under that name:

from django_service_specs import SpecRegistry

registry = SpecRegistry()
registry.register("invoices.create", create_spec)
registry.register("invoices.list", list_spec)

server.register_tools(
    registry,
    overrides={
        "invoices.create": {"description": "Create an invoice.", "scopes": ("billing",)},
        "invoices.list": {"description": "List invoices.", "paginate": True},
    },
)

An entry and a direct register_tool of the same spec are the same tool. An overrides key the registry does not hold is a ValueError, as a typo rather than a no-op, and an entry that is not a kernel ServiceSpec or SelectorSpec is refused as register_tool refuses it. A refusal of any entry registers none of them: every entry is built and checked first. It returns the bindings in registration order.

docs.title: Per-tool registration kwargs
docs.text:
Beyond description=, scopes= and server_arguments=, register_tool takes the facts of the MCP binding rather than of the operation: title, icons, annotations, meta, ui, content_kind, content_mime_type, include_structured_content, include_output_schema, task_policy, invalidates (service tools), paginate and max_page_size (selector tools), max_result_bytes, dispatch_timeout, always_listed, rate_limits and unknown_arguments. display_name and display_description are labels for in-process consumers, read off the binding and never sent on the wire. Each is also a key register_tools takes in overrides. Two of them decide what a caller is shown and may send:

  • unknown_arguments= — how arguments keys the spec does not declare are handled. It takes the kernel's UnknownArguments, and the inputSchema is the kernel's spec_input_schema under the same policy, so the closed schema is advertised exactly where the call refuses an undeclared name.
  • UnknownArguments.REJECT (default) — an undeclared key is refused with an isError validation_error result keyed by the key's name under detail ({"note": ["Unknown argument."]}), and the inputSchema advertises "additionalProperties": false.
  • UnknownArguments.IGNORE — undeclared keys are dropped before the spec sees them, and the inputSchema is open.
  • UnknownArguments.PASSTHROUGH — refused at registration with ImproperlyConfigured naming the tool, because the kernel never hands an undeclared argument to a callable. Declare the argument as a read and pass IGNORE or REJECT.

A paginated tool's page and limit are declared by the server and always known.

  • always_listed= — when SPEC_MCP["FILTER_LISTINGS_BY_PERMISSIONS"] is enabled, bindings are dropped from tools/list / resources/list / prompts/list when their permissions deny the current caller, and a tool is left out of tools/list whenever an operation-scope affordance refuses it right now (see below). Setting always_listed=True keeps the binding visible through both as a discovery aid; the permission and the affordance still gate the actual invocation. For a tool or a resource the permissions that deny are its spec's own checks, asked with no arguments; see Filtering listings by permissions.

docs.title: A tool that cannot run now is not listed
docs.text:
A service's affordances say when the operation is possible. A condition written as a callable is answered against the pool's seeds — user, progress, the call's call_context and any seed the server registers with pool_seeds= — and never against the call's arguments. So when a condition is unmet every call of the tool is refused, whatever the client sends. tools/list therefore asks each such condition, through the kernel's unmet_operation_affordance, and leaves the tool out while any is unmet:

from django_service_specs import Affordance, ServiceSpec

server.register_tool(
    ServiceSpec(
        service=close_period,
        affordances=[
            Affordance(
                code="books_closed",
                reason="The books for this period are already closed.",
                when=lambda user: user.ledger.is_open,
            ),
        ],
        permissions=[IsBookkeeper()],
    ),
    name="ledger.close_period",
    description="Close the current accounting period.",
)
  • Asked on every tools/list, with the user a call would use. A condition reads the transport's request from its call_context, as a call's condition does: the transport's own HttpRequest, carrying the token as mcp_token, with action the tool's name. It sees the token's user. It is not gated by FILTER_LISTINGS_BY_PERMISSIONS: that setting is off by default because a permission may read arguments that do not exist at list time, and a condition answered against the seeds cannot read arguments at all.
  • A condition on the row is never asked here. One written as an ORM expression (when=~Q(status="shipped")) has no row at list time; it is skipped without a query and goes on being answered per object at the call. A tool declaring only those is always listed.
  • Declaring nothing costs nothing. A pool is built only for a listed tool that declares a condition on the operation, from that tool's own call context, as its call builds one, so each registered seed's resolver runs once per such tool per listing. Each condition runs once per listing for its tool, so keep them and the seeds cheap. One that raises fails the listing, as it would fail the call.
  • Selector tools are never left out. A SelectorSpec's affordances names other operations to project onto its rows; it is not a condition on the read.
  • Resources and prompts are unaffected. A resource is a read, and a prompt holds no spec for an affordance to sit on.
  • The listing is advisory; the call is the authority. tools/call looks the tool up by name without consulting any listing, so a client holding an older one gets the refusal it would have got anyway: an isError result carrying the affordance's code (see Dispatch flow), not an unknown tool.

Keeping clients current. Nothing is cached on the server — each tools/list asks again — so the question is when a client asks:

  • A condition that flips on an event (an admin closes the books): announce it once the change has committed, and a client re-lists.

    from asgiref.sync import async_to_sync
from django.db import transaction
from django_spec_mcp import NotificationKind

transaction.on_commit(
    lambda: async_to_sync(server.notify_list_changed)(NotificationKind.TOOLS_LIST_CHANGED)
)

    This reaches a client only when a subscription broker is configured and the client speaks the modern era, the same two conditions listChanged is advertised on, and has opted in to toolsListChanged on its subscription. Without a broker it is a no-op, so it is safe to call unconditionally.

  • A condition that flips with the clock (a period ends at midnight): nothing announces it. The client sees it on its next tools/list, which one honouring the catalog's ttlMs may put off for up to CATALOG_CACHE_TTL_MS; a call made in between is refused with the code.

A listing that asked any condition is served with cacheScope: private, because it was answered for this caller and is no longer identical for every caller.

Saying why a tool is missing. A listing only leaves a tool out; nothing on the wire says which tools were left out or why. An in-process consumer can ask: MCPServer.unavailable_tools names each tool the listing omits with the Affordance that omitted it, from the same pass, so a model can be told the operation exists and why it cannot run now rather than guessing (see Full in-process transport).

docs.title: Tool annotations
docs.text:
Every tool advertises the MCP-standard ToolAnnotations hints, derived from what the server already knows about the tool's mutation profile — so downstream clients get correct readOnlyHint / destructiveHint without a hand-set flag:

  • Selector tools are reads → {"readOnlyHint": true}.
  • Service tools are mutations → {"readOnlyHint": false, "destructiveHint": true}.

destructiveHint / idempotentHint are spec-meaningful only when readOnlyHint is false, so a read-only tool emits neither.

A service tool also reads its spec's declared ServiceSpec.idempotent: idempotent=True advertises "idempotentHint": true, a declared False advertises false, and the default None (nothing declared) leaves the hint off, which a client reads as the MCP default of false.

Pass annotations= at registration to override or extend the derived hints — the explicit values win:

server.register_tool(
    mark_paid_spec,
    name="invoices.mark_paid",
    description="Mark an invoice as paid.",
    # A non-destructive mutation. Its idempotency is declared on the spec
    # (ServiceSpec(idempotent=True)), so it needs no hint here:
    annotations={"destructiveHint": False},
)

The merged bundle lands on binding.annotations and on the tools/list wire payload.

docs.title: Generic _meta
docs.text:
Separate from annotations — which is a closed, spec-defined set of client hints — the base protocol gives most wire objects a free-form _meta object. It is the extension namespace: each protocol extension owns a top-level key inside it, and a server may add its own.

Pass meta= at any registration surface (register_tool, a register_tools override, register_resource, register_ui_resource and register_prompt):

server.register_tool(
    list_invoices_spec,
    name="invoices.list",
    description="List invoices.",
    meta={"example.com/panel": {"href": "panel://invoices"}},
)

The bundle lands on binding.meta and is emitted verbatim under the "_meta" key of the binding's listing entry — tools/list, resources/list, resources/templates/list, prompts/list — and, for a resource, on the contents block resources/read returns. It is omitted entirely when empty.

Nothing here validates, reserves, or rewrites a key: the whole point of _meta is that its contents are opaque to the transport. On the tools/call result envelope _meta is per-call rather than per-binding, so it is a build_tool_result(..., meta=...) argument instead of something sourced from the binding.

docs.title: Transport-neutral invocation: call_tool
docs.text:
server.call_tool(name, arguments, *, user, request=None) invokes a registered tool off the HTTP / JSON-RPC path and returns the same ToolResult the wire handlers build. An in-process consumer — a bridge, an agent's toolset, a management command — uses it instead of re-implementing dispatch:

result = server.call_tool("invoices.create", {"number": "A-1"}, user=request.user)
result.structured_content  # the rendered payload

An agent is the common case; Connect a Pydantic-AI agent covers driving this server from one.

It runs the kernel's dispatch, as the wire does, so the spec-execution core (the spec's permissions, the argument check, the target lookup, the service or selector run, queryset shaping including filter_set, the retrieve nullability contract, pagination and the presenter) is the one every route shares rather than one reproduced here. The spec's permissions are asked of user before the arguments are checked, as on the wire, so a caller they refuse is told that rather than which argument it left out.

What it does not apply is the transport around the spec: there is no token in process, so the scopes= gate is not judged, and no rate limit is charged. Refused input (an undeclared argument under REJECT, a missing or invalid one), a service raising ServiceValidationError / ServiceError, a missing row and a presenter refusing a shape the caller sent come back as the isError results the wire serves. A denied permission raises the kernel's NotPermitted or PrincipalUnavailable, for the caller to map to its own wire. A service raising AdditionalInputRequired is a service_error result here, since there is no further round to ask in.

The request. request= is the caller's own Django request when there is one, often the very request a view is serving, so the call never writes its user to it. The call works on a copy whose user is the user= the call runs as: a view handing its own request keeps serving as its own user after the call, and two concurrent calls sharing one request each see their own. Apart from the user, the copy is the handed request for everything a call reads from it: the session, the body, the stream and the parsed GET, POST and FILES are the caller's, so a body a spec reads is read for the caller, a stream it drains is drained for the caller, and a body no spec reads stays unread for the view. Every other attribute starts as the very object the handed request holds: one a spec rebinds or deletes on the copy changes the copy alone, and one the caller sets once the call has its copy is not seen by it, but an object a spec mutates through one (META, the session, the message storage) is the caller's. Upload handlers Django creates during the call are bound to the handed request, so a handler reading request.user reads the caller's. The copy is an instance of a subclass of the handed request's class, so isinstance holds where type(request) is WSGIRequest does not, and it does not pickle. With no request handed, a minimal POST HttpRequest bearing user= is synthesised. The spec finds the copy, or the synthesised request, as call_context["request"], with no mcp_token on it, even when the handed request carried one: call_tool has no token.

docs.title: Full in-process transport: acall_tool / list_tools
docs.text:
call_tool is the spec core. When an in-process consumer needs the whole transport — exactly what a remote MCP client sees — MCPServer exposes two async-friendly siblings that route through the same wire handlers:

page = server.list_tools(user=request.user, request=request)  # one tools/list page
page["tools"]  # the inputSchema per tool
page["nextCursor"]  # pass back to list_tools(cursor, ...) to paginate

result = await server.acall_tool("invoices.list", {"page": 1}, user=request.user, request=request)
result["structuredContent"]  # the wire's result payload (dict, not ToolResult)
  • list_tools(cursor=None, *, user, request=None, scopes=None) returns one page of the tool catalog with the same inputSchema (a paginated tool's page and limit and the additionalProperties policy included), the same FILTER_LISTINGS_BY_PERMISSIONS per-caller filter, the same availability filter, and the same opaque-cursor pagination the HTTP transport uses. alist_tools is its twin for an event loop, running the listing in Django's thread-sensitive executor.
  • acall_tool(name, arguments=None, *, user, request=None, scopes=None) invokes a tool with the full transport applied: the scopes= gate and the rate limits — everything call_tool deliberately omits. It returns the wire's dict payload (content / structuredContent / isError) or a JsonRpcError for a protocol fault (unknown tool, malformed arguments shape, denied permission).

Both build the call context internally from user + request, handling a handed request as call_tool does: a copy bearing the call's user, or a minimal request synthesised when request is None. acall_tool carries a token built from user= and scopes= on that request as mcp_token, so a tool gated by scopes= is invokable in-process just as it is on the wire. JsonRpcError and JsonRpcErrorCode are re-exported from the package root so a consumer can branch on faults. This is the surface an in-process MCP bridge consumes to run this server's tools with HTTP-equivalent semantics.

A consumer that lists once and follows availability per step. An agent loop offers its model tools on every step, and whether a tool can run may change between steps. Re-listing each step would rebuild every schema to learn a few booleans, so the transport splits the two:

page = server.list_tools(user=request.user, request=request, include_unavailable=True)
# ... build the model's tool definitions from page["tools"] once, then each step:
missing = await server.aunavailable_tools(user=request.user, request=request)
offered = [tool for tool in definitions if tool.name not in missing]
for name, affordance in missing.items():
    ...  # tell the model: `name` exists but cannot run now, because affordance.reason
