direct_call_tool bypasses the model loop, which makes it the fastest way to confirm the wire is working before you spend a token on it.

docs.title: Add rate limiting to a binding
docs.text:
MCPRateLimit is a Protocol — anything with a single consume(request, token) -> int | None method qualifies. The return value is the suggested retry-after-in-seconds when the limit has been hit, or None to allow the call.

rate_limits= on register_tool, register_resource and register_prompt is what limits an MCP call.

The shipped FixedWindowRateLimit is backed by django.core.cache and is the right choice for most Django deployments — the cache is already shared across worker processes when you're running anything serious.

from django_service_specs import ServiceSpec, Unrestricted

from django_spec_mcp import MCPServer
from django_spec_mcp.auth.rate_limits.fixed_window_rate_limit import (
    FixedWindowRateLimit,
)

server = MCPServer(name="my-app", auth_backend=my_auth_backend)

server.register_tool(
    ServiceSpec(service=create_invoice, permissions=[Unrestricted()]),
    name="invoices.create",
    rate_limits=[
        FixedWindowRateLimit(max_calls=120, per_seconds=60, namespace="burst"),
        FixedWindowRateLimit(max_calls=10_000, per_seconds=86_400, namespace="daily"),
    ],
)

Limits are AND-combined — denial from any limiter immediately rejects the call. The handler stops at the first denial (no point further consuming quota when the call is going to fail).

docs.title: Wire shape
docs.text:
Denial returns JSON-RPC error code -32005 RATE_LIMITED with data.retryAfter set to the suggested seconds:

{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "error": {
    "code": -32005,
    "message": "Rate limit exceeded",
    "data": {"retryAfter": 42}
  }
}

MCP clients that respect this should back off accordingly. Misbehaving clients keep hitting the same limit; the cache counter is per-bucket so the counter doesn't grow unbounded.

docs.title: Custom keys
docs.text:
The default FixedWindowRateLimit keys per authenticated user (or REMOTE_ADDR for anonymous requests). Override with a callable:

def per_org_key(request, token) -> str:
    return f"org:{token.user.organization_id}"


server.register_tool(
    spec,
    name="invoices.create",
    rate_limits=[
        FixedWindowRateLimit(max_calls=10_000, per_seconds=60, key=per_org_key),
    ],
)

docs.title: Choosing a scheme
docs.text:
Three implementations ship in django_spec_mcp.auth.rate_limits:

  • FixedWindowRateLimit — bucketed counters, atomic via cache.add + cache.incr. Cheaper, but a client can issue 2 * max_calls across the bucket boundary.
  • SlidingWindowRateLimit — list of timestamps in cache, pruned on every call. Smoother (limits the rolling-window rate, not bucket count), at the cost of a small read-modify-write race under concurrency.
  • TokenBucketRateLimit — bucket of tokens that refills continuously at refill_per_second. Burst-friendly: a full bucket absorbs a sudden burst of capacity requests, then the steady-state rate clamps to refill_per_second. Useful when consumers naturally batch.
from django_spec_mcp.auth.rate_limits import (
    FixedWindowRateLimit,
    SlidingWindowRateLimit,
    TokenBucketRateLimit,
)

server.register_tool(
    spec,
    name="invoices.create",
    rate_limits=[
        # Steady-state 1 call/sec, but absorb bursts up to 60.
        TokenBucketRateLimit(capacity=60, refill_per_second=1.0),
    ],
)

All three share the same consume(request, token) -> int | None signature, so swapping is a one-line change. The shipped classes are read-modify-write on django.core.cache — for strict atomicity under heavy concurrency, back the limiter with a Redis-Lua script implementing the same Protocol.

docs.title: Implementing your own
docs.text:
For leaky buckets, GCRA, distributed Lua-backed schemes etc. — implement the Protocol against your storage of choice:

from django.http import HttpRequest

from django_spec_mcp import TokenInfo


class LeakyBucketRateLimit:
    """Naive sketch — production should use redis-py with Lua for atomicity."""

    def __init__(self, *, capacity: int, leak_per_second: float) -> None:
        self._capacity = capacity
        self._leak = leak_per_second

    def consume(self, request: HttpRequest, token: TokenInfo) -> int | None: ...

Pass it to a binding the same way:

server.register_tool(
    spec,
    name="invoices.create",
    rate_limits=[LeakyBucketRateLimit(capacity=60, leak_per_second=1)],
)

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Limiters are constructed once per binding at registration time — shared across all dispatches. Keep __init__ cheap.
  • State that crosses requests must live in shared storage, not on the instance. FixedWindowRateLimit follows this rule (Django cache); custom limiters must too if they're going to work under multiple worker processes.
  • The default Django locmem cache is process-local. In production, use Memcached or Redis so all workers see the same counter.
  • consume must be a plain def, on both transports — see Add a custom permission. An async def consume raises ImproperlyConfigured: nothing awaits it, and a coroutine is not None, so every call would be denied with the coroutine object standing in for retryAfter. Wrap any awaiting in asgiref.sync.async_to_sync inside the method.

docs.title: Multi-worker SSE with Redis
docs.text:
The default InMemorySSEBroker works for single-process deployments — one ASGI worker, one event loop, no fan-out concerns. Multi-worker setups need an out-of-process broker so any worker can deliver a notify(...) to whichever worker is holding the streaming GET.

The shipped RedisSSEBroker is the production answer.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install "django-spec-mcp[redis]"

Pulls in redis>=5.0 (which provides redis.asyncio).

docs.title: Wire it up
docs.text:
myproject/mcp.py
from redis.asyncio import Redis

from django_spec_mcp import MCPServer
from django_spec_mcp.transport.redis_sse_broker import RedisSSEBroker


redis_client = Redis.from_url("redis://localhost:6379/0", decode_responses=False)

server = MCPServer(
    name="my-app",
    sse_broker=RedisSSEBroker(redis_client),
)

That's the only change. server.async_urls will now route SSE through Redis pub/sub. The wire shape is identical from the client's perspective — GET /mcp/ still streams data: events; await server.notify(...) still returns whether a subscriber was attached.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
For each session that opens a streaming GET, the broker spawns a background asyncio.Task that subscribes to the per-session Redis channel (spec-mcp:sse:<session_id> by default). The task pumps incoming pub/sub messages onto a per-session asyncio.Queue, which the streaming generator consumes — same interface as the in-memory broker.

publish is a single Redis PUBLISH call. Any worker that calls await server.notify(session_id, ...) reaches the right session because every worker subscribes to the same channel.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Single subscriber per session. Same contract as the in-memory broker. If you scale to multiple workers and a session reconnects after a network hiccup, the new worker's subscriber replaces the old. The dropped subscriber's task on the original worker eventually unwinds (cancelled by unsubscribe or by Redis client shutdown).
  • Replay is opt-in. Messages published while no subscriber was attached are dropped unless you configure an SSEReplayBuffer — see the Last-Event-ID resume recipe.
  • Channel-prefix isolation. Pass channel_prefix="env-staging" (or similar) to keep dev / staging / prod traffic in the same Redis instance from cross-talking.
  • Client lifecycle is yours. Close the Redis client during ASGI lifespan shutdown — the broker doesn't own it.

docs.title: Custom brokers
docs.text: RedisSSEBroker is just a class that implements the SSEBroker Protocol (four methods: subscribe, unsubscribe, publish, has_subscriber). NATS-, Kafka-, RabbitMQ-backed brokers fit the same interface — just keep the single-subscriber-per-session contract.

docs.title: Register tools from a shared spec registry
docs.text:
If MCP is the only way your project exposes its specs, keep calling register_tool directly — this recipe buys you nothing.

It pays off when the same specs are exposed over more than one transport: MCP here, plus an agent toolset, plus HTTP views. Each transport has to be told which specs it exposes, so you end up writing the list once per transport — and the lists drift. A spec gets added to the MCP wiring and forgotten in the agent's, or the same operation ends up named create_order here and something else there.

SpecRegistry, from django-service-specs, is the one declaration site. MCPServer.register_tools is the MCP end of it.

docs.title: Declare once
docs.text:
# orders/registry.py
from django_service_specs import SpecRegistry

registry = SpecRegistry()


# orders/apps.py
from django.apps import AppConfig


class OrdersConfig(AppConfig):
    name = "orders"

    def ready(self) -> None:
        from orders import specs
        from orders.registry import registry

        registry.register("list_orders", specs.list_orders, tags=("read", "public"))
        registry.register("get_order", specs.get_order, tags=("read", "public"))
        registry.register("refund_order", specs.refund_order, tags=("write", "admin"))

The registry holds only what every transport agrees on — which spec, its canonical name, its tags.

docs.title: Register them as tools
docs.text:
# orders/mcp.py
from django_spec_mcp import MCPServer

from orders.registry import registry

server = MCPServer(name="orders", auth_backend=my_auth_backend)
server.register_tools(registry)

Each entry becomes a tool through register_tool, under its registry name: a ServiceSpec is a service tool, a SelectorSpec a selector tool. Registration order is the registry's order, so tools/list stays stable. An entry that is not a kernel ServiceSpec or SelectorSpec is refused with a TypeError naming the tool, as register_tool refuses it.

This is a source for the server's own ToolRegistry, not a replacement for it. Every tool still lands as a normal binding, and names still share the one MCP tool namespace — a name the server already holds is refused.

docs.title: Keep the MCP knobs where they belong
docs.text:
The registry is deliberately transport-agnostic: it has no idea what paginate or annotations mean. Everything MCP-specific stays here, per tool, via overrides:

server.register_tools(
    registry,
    overrides={
        "list_orders": {
            "paginate": True,
            "description": "List orders, newest first by default.",
        },
        "refund_order": {
            "annotations": {"title": "Refund an order"},
            "scopes": ("orders:write",),
        },
    },
)

Each value is the keyword arguments of register_tool for that entry, so anything it accepts works — title, include_output_schema, rate_limits, server_arguments, and the rest.

A fact about the operation is not an MCP knob, though, even when MCP has a hint for it. Whether repeating a refund is safe is true of the refund on every transport, so it is declared once on the spec, where each transport reads it:

# orders/specs.py
from django_service_specs import Parameter, Parameters, ServiceSpec

refund_order = ServiceSpec(
    service=refund_order_service,
    reads=Parameters([Parameter("order_pk", "integer", required=True)]),
    permissions=[IsOrderAdmin()],
    # Declared, not left unsaid: a second call refunds again.
    idempotent=False,
)

The server turns that declaration into "idempotentHint": false on the tool. A spec that declares nothing (idempotent=None, the default) gets no hint, and an annotations= override still wins over the derived value. See Tool annotations.

docs.title: What the entry already says
docs.text:
A spec declares what a caller has to send as its reads: a route capture, a query value or a body field is a Parameter like any other, so the entry mounted here and in an in-process agent toolset advertises the same arguments. Every transport reads them off the spec:

from django_service_specs import Parameter, Parameters, SelectorKind, SelectorSpec

orders_spec = SelectorSpec(
    kind=SelectorKind.LIST,
    selector=list_project_orders,
    reads=Parameters([Parameter("project_pk", "integer", required=True)]),
    presenter=ORDER,
    permissions=[IsProjectMember()],
)
registry.register("list_project_orders", orders_spec)

server.register_tools(
    registry,
    overrides={"list_project_orders": {"paginate": True}},
)  # the tool takes project_pk, declared once

To add a read to an entry registered elsewhere, re-declare the spec it holds with dataclasses.replace and mount the registry replace returns:

from dataclasses import replace

spec = registry.get("list_project_orders").spec
scoped = registry.subset("list_project_orders").replace(
    "list_project_orders",
    replace(
        spec,
        reads=Parameters([*spec.reads, Parameter("since", "string", format="date-time")]),
    ),
)

server.register_tools(
    scoped,
    overrides={"list_project_orders": {"paginate": True}},
)  # the tool takes project_pk and since

register_tools passes nothing about an entry's reads: register_tool reads the spec's own, so the spec above registered with register_tool(spec, ...) is the same tool, advertising the same arguments.

docs.title: Answering an argument for the caller: server_arguments
docs.text:
A mount that already knows an argument - the project this server is scoped to, say - answers it with a ServerArguments from django_service_specs, as an override like any other:

from django_service_specs import ServerArguments

server.register_tools(
    scoped,  # the registry above, whose entry reads project_pk and since
    overrides={
        "list_project_orders": {
            "paginate": True,
            "server_arguments": ServerArguments(
                values={"project_pk": 7},  # always this project
                withheld=frozenset({"since"}),  # never the caller's; the default applies
            ),
        },
    },
)

Both names leave the tool's inputSchema and its required list, so the model is never asked for them. A caller sending one anyway has its value dropped before anything reads it, and the server logs the tool and the argument names at WARNING, never the values. Registration checks the binding: a name the spec does not declare, a value its declared type refuses, and a withheld name with no default each raise ImproperlyConfigured naming the tool. See server-supplied arguments for the full rule.

The values are fixed for the life of the server. A value computed per request, such as a project read off the signed-in user, is not something server_arguments carries; scope it in a pool seed, a kwargs= provider or a permission check.

Three things fail loudly rather than quietly, and a refusal of any entry registers none of them:

  • An overrides key naming a spec the registry doesn't hold raises ValueError. A typo would otherwise be a silent no-op.
  • A knob that belongs to the other kind of tool — paginate on a ServiceSpec, invalidates on a SelectorSpec — raises ImproperlyConfigured naming the tool.
  • A key register_tool does not take raises TypeError.

docs.title: Two mounts, two surfaces
docs.text:
The registry does not force one surface. Filtered views (by_tag, subset) each return a new registry, so a multi-mount deployment feeds each server its own projection with no shared state:

internal = MCPServer(name="orders-internal", auth_backend=my_auth_backend)
public = MCPServer(name="orders-public", auth_backend=my_auth_backend)

internal.register_tools(registry)  # everything
public.register_tools(registry.by_tag("public"))  # reads only

Independent registries work too, when the surfaces have nothing in common: names are unique within a registry, so two registries may reuse one.

docs.title: Permissions are not bypassed
docs.text:
A spec declaring no permissions at all never reaches this server: SpecRegistry.register refuses it, because no transport has a policy it could inherit. [Unrestricted()] registers, and says the operation is open out loud. register_tools calls the same register_tool you would have called, so every check a direct registration runs applies to each entry.

Bulk registration is a convenience, not a way to register a surface you haven't secured. A scopes= override adds an OAuth scope gate to an entry, beside the spec's own permissions rather than in place of them:

server.register_tools(
    registry,
    overrides={"refund_order": {"scopes": ("orders:write",)}},
)

docs.title: A selector tool with filtering, ordering, and pagination
docs.text:
A service tool wraps a mutation: register_tool with a kernel ServiceSpec runs the spec's service callable, inside transaction.atomic() by default, and presents its result.

For reads you want a different shape. A "list invoices" tool is read-only and benefits from filtering, ordering, and pagination — none of which belong inside the selector. A LIST SelectorSpec keeps the selector tiny (return a queryset); the spec's filter_set narrows and orders it, and paginate=True at registration pages it.

arguments → the kernel's argument check (the spec's reads, the FilterSet's filters)
          → run the selector
          → FilterSet(data=…).qs    (if spec.filter_set)
          → FilterSet applies ordering  (if it declares an OrderingFilter)
          → paginate                (if paginate=True)
          → the presenter, per row
          → ToolResult

Each piece is opt-in. A SelectorSpec with no filter set registered without paginate behaves like a plain RPC read.

docs.title: Install django-filter
docs.text:
filter_set= takes a django-filter FilterSet, which the kernel's filter extra installs:

pip install "django-service-specs[filter]"

Nothing in this package imports it, so a project with no filter set does not need it.

docs.title: Define the pieces
docs.text:
A model:

# invoices/models.py
from django.db import models


class Invoice(models.Model):
    number = models.CharField(max_length=32, unique=True)
    amount_cents = models.PositiveIntegerField()
    sent = models.BooleanField(default=False)
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)

What a row renders as, through the kernel's DataclassPresenter:

# invoices/shapes.py
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime


@dataclass
class InvoiceOutput:
    id: int
    number: str
    amount_cents: int
    sent: bool
    created_at: datetime

A scoped selector — returns a raw queryset, no filtering or ordering:

# invoices/selectors.py
from django.db.models import QuerySet

from invoices.models import Invoice


def list_invoices(*, user) -> QuerySet[Invoice]:
    """Return every invoice the caller is allowed to see."""
    return Invoice.objects.for_user(user)  # your scoping manager

A FilterSet describing the parametric reads the tool exposes:

# invoices/filters.py
import django_filters

from invoices.models import Invoice


class InvoiceFilterSet(django_filters.FilterSet):
    sent = django_filters.BooleanFilter()
    min_amount = django_filters.NumberFilter(field_name="amount_cents", lookup_expr="gte")
    max_amount = django_filters.NumberFilter(field_name="amount_cents", lookup_expr="lte")
    created_after = django_filters.DateTimeFilter(field_name="created_at", lookup_expr="gte")
    # Ordering is declared here, like any other filter. The kernel reads it
    # into the tool's `inputSchema` as a choice over the names on the left —
    # the public vocabulary, not the ORM paths behind them.
    ordering = django_filters.OrderingFilter(
        fields=(("created_at", "created"), ("amount_cents", "amount")),
    )

    class Meta:
        model = Invoice
        fields = ["sent", "min_amount", "max_amount", "created_after"]

docs.title: Register the selector tool
docs.text:
from django_service_specs import DataclassPresenter, SelectorKind, SelectorSpec, Unrestricted

from django_spec_mcp import MCPServer
from invoices.filters import InvoiceFilterSet
from invoices.selectors import list_invoices
from invoices.shapes import InvoiceOutput

server = MCPServer(name="invoicing", auth_backend=my_auth_backend)

server.register_tool(
    SelectorSpec(
        kind=SelectorKind.LIST,
        selector=list_invoices,
        filter_set=InvoiceFilterSet,
        presenter=DataclassPresenter(InvoiceOutput),
        permissions=[Unrestricted()],
    ),
    name="invoices.list",
    description="List invoices, optionally filtered / ordered / paginated.",
    paginate=True,
)

filter_set lives on the SelectorSpec, so the same declaration drives every transport that serves the spec — declare the filterable shape once. Its filters are reads: the kernel reads each one as an optional Parameter, so the inputSchema lists it and the closed argument set admits it. Ordering rides along with it: nothing about ordering appears on the registration call, because the OrderingFilter already declared it. paginate is the one MCP-only pipeline mechanic left here.

A LIST selector tool registered without paginate=True warns UnboundedListWarning, and SPEC_MCP["REQUIRE_LIST_PAGINATION"] refuses it: an unpaged list grows with the table until one call no longer fits a client's context.

docs.title: Two ways to offer ordering
docs.text:
Ordering is not a registration knob, and there are two channels that need none. Both reach the tool's inputSchema, so one declaration serves every transport.

  1. An OrderingFilter on the FilterSet — the one above. Prefer this wherever there is a FilterSet: the value is checked against a published set of choices before anything reaches the ORM, and the choices are consumer-facing names rather than column paths.

  2. A sort read the spec declares itself — for a project with no django-filter dependency. A Parameter with choices is checked before the selector runs, so only the names you list reach it:

    from django_service_specs import Parameter, Parameters

SORTS = {"newest": "-created_at", "amount": "amount_cents"}


def list_invoices(*, user, sort: str = "newest"):
    """List the caller's invoices, newest first by default."""
    return Invoice.objects.for_user(user).order_by(SORTS[sort])


SelectorSpec(
    kind=SelectorKind.LIST,
    selector=list_invoices,
    reads=Parameters([Parameter("sort", "string", choices=tuple(SORTS))]),
    presenter=DataclassPresenter(InvoiceOutput),
    permissions=[Unrestricted()],
)

Do not name that read page or limit

Those two names belong to a paginated tool's pipeline, which takes both from the arguments before the selector runs. A spec declaring a read named either is refused when it is registered with paginate=True. A RETRIEVE tool cannot paginate, so its selector may take either name. ordering is not reserved: name a read ordering if that reads best.

docs.title: Generated inputSchema
docs.text:
tools/list advertises the merged shape:

{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "sent": {"type": "boolean"},
    "min_amount": {
      "type": "string",
      "format": "decimal",
      "minimum": -1e50,
      "maximum": 1e50,
      "description": "Matches `amount_cents` with the `gte` lookup."
    },
    "max_amount": {
      "type": "string",
      "format": "decimal",
      "minimum": -1e50,
      "maximum": 1e50,
      "description": "Matches `amount_cents` with the `lte` lookup."
    },
    "created_after": {
      "type": "string",
      "format": "date-time",
      "description": "Matches `created_at` with the `gte` lookup."
    },
    "ordering": {
      "type": "array",
      "items": {"type": "string", "enum": ["created", "-created", "amount", "-amount"]},
      "maxItems": 1000
    },
    "page": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1},
    "limit": {"type": "integer", "minimum": 1, "maximum": 100}
  },
  "additionalProperties": false
}

Filter properties are always optional — they narrow the queryset but aren't required to call the tool. Ordering takes a list of names, each ascending (field) or descending (-field): ["-amount"] is the largest first. page defaults to 1 and limit to 100 when the model omits it.

A number filter is a decimal string, which its form field reads exactly; a JSON number is still taken. The description on min_amount, max_amount and created_after is derived, not written: where a filter's own name does not give away which column it matches or with which lookup, the kernel states both. A filter whose name, field and lookup already agree — sent — says nothing extra. The kernel's declaring guide has the full filter-to-Parameter mapping.

limit's maximum is the effective MAX_PAGE_SIZE — the server-wide setting, or the max_page_size= passed at registration. It is advertised here and clamped at dispatch, and it disappears from the schema entirely when the bound is None. It is unrelated to PAGE_SIZE, which bounds listing calls such as tools/list and never reaches a selector tool's limit.

docs.title: Paginated response shape
docs.text:
When paginate=True, tools/call wraps the presented rows in a pagination envelope:

{
  "items": [<presented rows>],
  "page": 1,
  "totalPages": 7,
  "hasNext": true
}

Without paginate, the response is the presented list directly. Choose based on how many rows your selector can return — paginate as soon as the list could outgrow a single tool-call response.

docs.title: Arguments beside the filters
docs.text:
filter_set only describes the filter shape. If the tool also needs arguments that are not filters, declare them as the spec's reads: they join the FilterSet's filters in the inputSchema, and the selector receives each one by name.

from django_service_specs import Parameter, Parameters


def list_invoices(*, user, include_drafts: bool = False):
    invoices = Invoice.objects.for_user(user)
    return invoices if include_drafts else invoices.exclude(number__startswith="DRAFT-")


server.register_tool(
    SelectorSpec(
        kind=SelectorKind.LIST,
        selector=list_invoices,
        reads=Parameters([Parameter("include_drafts", "boolean", default=False)]),
        filter_set=InvoiceFilterSet,
        presenter=DataclassPresenter(InvoiceOutput),
        permissions=[Unrestricted()],
    ),
    name="invoices.list",
    description="List invoices, optionally with drafts.",
    paginate=True,
)

FilterSet-driven filters are applied after the selector returns its base queryset. A read named like one of the FilterSet's filters but declared differently is refused when the spec is built.

docs.title: When to reach for a service tool instead
docs.text: If the operation creates / updates / deletes rows, register a ServiceSpec. A service tool runs inside transaction.atomic() (by default) and presents the service's return, not a queryset pipeline. Selector tools are the read-shaped sibling — they should never have side effects.

docs.title: Resume dropped SSE streams with Last-Event-ID
docs.text:
The MCP transport supports the standard SSE Last-Event-ID header so clients that drop a streaming connection can reconnect and receive the events they missed. This is opt-in: pass an SSEReplayBuffer to MCPServer(sse_replay_buffer=...) and every event published via await server.notify(...) is recorded with a monotonic ID before fan-out, then replayed on the client's next GET if it arrives carrying Last-Event-ID.

Without a buffer, the wire shape is unchanged — no id: lines, and a client that sends Last-Event-ID is silently ignored (no replay, fresh live stream).

docs.title: Single-process: InMemorySSEReplayBuffer
docs.text:
Suitable when you run a single ASGI worker. State lives on the buffer instance, sized to a fixed-cap deque per session.

myproject/mcp.py
from django_spec_mcp import MCPServer
from django_spec_mcp.transport.in_memory_sse_replay_buffer import (
    InMemorySSEReplayBuffer,
)

server = MCPServer(
    name="my-app",
    sse_replay_buffer=InMemorySSEReplayBuffer(max_events=2048),
)

max_events caps per-session retention. Events older than that drop off the back when new ones arrive — a client that disconnects for very long and replays from a buried event sees a partial replay (best-effort).

docs.title: Multi-worker: RedisSSEReplayBuffer
docs.text:
Pair this with RedisSSEBroker so any worker can both publish the live event and serve the replay request. The buffer is backed by a Redis Stream per session: XADD MAXLEN ~ N for record (capped, approximate trimming), XRANGE (<id> + for replay.

myproject/mcp.py
from redis.asyncio import Redis

from django_spec_mcp import MCPServer
from django_spec_mcp.transport.redis_sse_broker import RedisSSEBroker
from django_spec_mcp.transport.redis_sse_replay_buffer import (
    RedisSSEReplayBuffer,
)


client = Redis.from_url("redis://localhost:6379/0")

server = MCPServer(
    name="my-app",
    sse_broker=RedisSSEBroker(client),
    sse_replay_buffer=RedisSSEReplayBuffer(client, max_events=4096),
)

The two collaborators are independent: you could pair an in-memory broker with a Redis buffer, or vice versa. They're decoupled because brokers handle live fan-out and buffers handle resume — different concerns, different storage trade-offs.

docs.title: What the wire looks like
docs.text:
With a buffer wired in, every notify produces an SSE frame carrying both id: and data::

id: 0000000000000007
data: {"event":"job-finished","jobId":42}

id: 0000000000000008
data: {"event":"job-finished","jobId":43}

On reconnect the client sends:

Last-Event-ID: 0000000000000007

…and the server replays event 8 (and any later events) before resuming live mode. Browser EventSource does this automatically; programmatic SSE clients should preserve the latest id: they received and echo it back on retry.

docs.title: Choosing max_events
docs.text:
Pick a number that covers your worst-case disconnect window times your peak event rate per session. Examples:

  • "5-minute reconnect window, 10 events/sec peak" → max_events ≥ 3000.
  • "1-minute reconnect window, 1 event/sec average" → max_events ≥ 60 (round up for headroom).

Per-session, so total memory scales with (active sessions) × max_events × avg_payload_size. The Redis variant is also bounded, but trims approximately: Redis shortens a stream only by dropping whole internal nodes, so each session keeps at least its newest max_events events and less than one node more. A node closes at whichever limit it reaches first, stream-node-max-entries (100 by default) or stream-node-max-bytes (4096 by default), so the margin is under 100 events and under about 4 KB per session. Budget Redis memory for max_events × avg_payload_size + ~4 KB per session.

The byte limit is usually the one that closes a node. Only events under about 30 bytes each fill one by count, leaving up to 99 extra; from about a hundred bytes up a node fills by size well before that, and once events are over about 2 KB each node holds one and trimming is effectively exact. One approximate trim also removes at most 10,000 entries (100 × stream-node-max-entries), so after a deploy lowers max_events on a long stream the first few writes leave it above the new bound before it catches up.

docs.title: Custom buffers
docs.text: SSEReplayBuffer is a small Protocol — three methods: record, replay, forget. Implement it against any storage you like (PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY, NATS JetStream, Kafka with a consumer group key, …). Pass your instance via sse_replay_buffer= and the rest of the package works unchanged.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Bounded retention. A client that disconnects for hours and tries to resume from an evicted ID will get a partial replay. The MCP spec is silent on how the client should detect this; in practice clients treat any successful resume as "OK" and rely on application-level consistency (e.g. a follow-up tools/call to fetch latest state).
  • DELETE forgets the buffer. When a client tears the session down with DELETE /mcp/, the transport calls buffer.forget(session_id) so dead sessions don't accumulate state. Buffers can no-op this if they prefer TTL-based eviction.
  • No replay without a buffer. This is a deliberate v1 default — most deployments don't need resume, and recording every event has cost. Opt in when you need it.

docs.title: Swap the session store
docs.text:
By default MCPServer uses DjangoCacheSessionStore — sessions live in django.core.cache, which works in multi-process deployments without extra infra. Two situations call for swapping it:

  • Tests want a clean, per-instance store so test ordering doesn't leak state.
  • Production at scale may want sessions in Redis directly (so they survive cache evictions) or backed by a persistent table.

docs.title: In tests: per-instance in-memory store
docs.text:
from django_spec_mcp import MCPServer
from django_spec_mcp.transport.in_memory_session_store import InMemorySessionStore

server = MCPServer(name="test", session_store=InMemorySessionStore())

The InMemorySessionStore keeps state on the instance, so multiple servers in one process don't share sessions. (This is one of the reasons the package forbids module/class-level mutable state — see CLAUDE.md.)

docs.title: In production: a custom store
docs.text:
Implement the SessionStore Protocol (four methods, no other contract). Every session is bound to the principal that initialized it: create receives a keyword-only principal_id and owner returns it — the transport compares it on every POST / GET / DELETE and treats a wrong-principal presentation exactly like an unknown session (404):

from django_spec_mcp.transport.types.session_store import SessionStore


class RedisSessionStore:
    def __init__(self, redis_client, ttl_seconds: int = 86400) -> None:
        self._redis = redis_client
        self._ttl = ttl_seconds

    def create(self, *, principal_id: str) -> str:
        import secrets

        token = secrets.token_urlsafe(24)
        self._redis.set(f"mcp:session:{token}", principal_id, ex=self._ttl)
        return token

    def exists(self, session_id: str) -> bool:
        return self._redis.exists(f"mcp:session:{session_id}") == 1

    def owner(self, session_id: str) -> str | None:
        value = self._redis.get(f"mcp:session:{session_id}")
        return value.decode() if value is not None else None

    def destroy(self, session_id: str) -> None:
        self._redis.delete(f"mcp:session:{session_id}")

Pass the instance when you build the server:

server = MCPServer(name="my-app", session_store=RedisSessionStore(redis_client))

An async def store belongs to server.async_urls only

The session store is the one collaborator the async transport genuinely awaits, so writing create / owner / destroy as async def is correct — under ASGI. Mount that same store under server.urls and the sync transport raises ImproperlyConfigured, naming the store and the method.

It refuses rather than proceeding because an un-awaited coroutine matches no principal and is not a usable session id: every request would answer "re-initialize", create would hand the client the repr of a coroutine as its Mcp-Session-Id, and destroy — whose return value nobody inspects — would silently leave the session alive. Pick one transport per store, or write it def and use it under both.

Namespace it if you mount more than one server

The default DjangoCacheSessionStore keys its entries under the server's url_namespace, so two mounts can't see each other's sessions. A store you build yourself is yours to namespace — give each server its own key space, or a session minted at /public/mcp will satisfy /internal/mcp.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
Autodocs sourced from the package itself via mkdocstrings. Every entry is generated from the live source — nothing duplicated by hand.

  • MCPServer — the public entry point.
  • Protocol types — JSON-RPC envelope, MCP message types, error codes.
  • Registries — ToolRegistry, ResourceRegistry, bindings, session stores.
  • Auth — backends, permissions, response builders.
  • Output — encode_json, build_tool_result.
  • Testing — assert_tool_result_conforms, for a consumer's own suite.
  • Settings — every SPEC_MCP key, its default, and the per-server override.

docs.title: Auth
docs.text:
Backends, response builders, rate limits, and the RFC 9728 protected-resource metadata view.

A tool or resource is guarded by its spec's own permissions, the kernel's PermissionCheck, and by the scopes= gate at registration; see Who may call a tool. A prompt or an interactive view takes the same kernel checks through permissions=, each handed the prompt's or view's binding as the spec, and the same scopes=; see Prompts and views.

docs.title: MCPAuthBackend
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

Pluggable authentication for the MCP transport.

The transport calls authenticate on every request; returning None signals "no valid credentials" and the transport emits a 401 whose WWW-Authenticate comes from www_authenticate_challenge. protected_resource_metadata powers the /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource view (RFC 9728); the PRM view calls .to_dict() on the returned dataclass for the wire shape.

The backend is the resource server's half of OAuth: the authorization server that issues the tokens publishes its own metadata, so nothing here describes it.

Backends MUST be safe to instantiate without arguments — settings-driven configuration belongs inside the backend's own module.

docs.title: TokenInfo dataclass
docs.text:
Authenticated principal carried alongside an MCP request.

Backends construct this once per request and attach it to the Django HttpRequest (as request.mcp_token). A binding's scope gate reads its scopes, and a spec's PermissionCheck reads it off the request in call_context.

Attributes:

Name Type Description user Any

The resolved Django user, or an AnonymousUser equivalent. Any because the user model is project-defined.

scopes tuple[str, ...]

OAuth scopes proven by the bearer token.

audience str | None

The aud claim. RFC 8707 requires it to match the canonical /mcp URL; backends own that comparison.

raw Any

Backend-specific opaque payload — the AccessToken row, the JWT claims dict — for advanced use cases.

docs.title: SelfChecking
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

An auth backend that can say whether it is able to serve requests.

Deliberately a second protocol rather than a method on :class:~django_spec_mcp.auth.types.auth_backend.MCPAuthBackend. Adding it there would make it required, and a backend already written against the four-method protocol would stop satisfying it -- so the one thing this exists to prevent, a transport mounted with a backend that cannot run, would be bought by breaking every backend anyone has already written.

Structural and runtime-checkable, so a backend opts in by having the method and nothing has to register anywhere. A backend that does not implement it is treated as ready, which is the right default: needing no setup is the ordinary case, and a backend that needs some is the one able to say so.

It is called when the server is mounted, and that is the whole point. A backend becomes load-bearing at the moment HTTP requests become possible, not when the server object is built: an in-process server -- call_tool, list_tools, the in-process route django-ag-ui uses -- never authenticates anything, so requiring a backend's optional dependency to construct one would refuse a supported deployment. Mounting is the earliest point at which the requirement is real, and it is still startup: server.urls runs while the URLConf is imported, so manage.py check reaches it and a missing dependency is a refusal at boot rather than a 500 on the first request.

check_configuration raises -- ImproperlyConfigured, naming what is missing and how to supply it -- or returns None. It must not return a bool: a caller that has to interpret a False has been given an error that knows more than it says.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text: This package ships no backend that verifies tokens; a project writes its own (Writing your own backend). A backend of its own compares the token's audience with audience_matches, the exact comparison RFC 8707 asks for, and builds its 401 challenge with bearer_challenge.

docs.title: AllowAnyBackend
docs.text:
Development / test backend that authenticates every request as anonymous.

DO NOT use in production. The protected_resource_metadata payload is intentionally minimal so misconfiguration is loud rather than silent.

docs.title: audience_matches
docs.text:
audience_matches(token_audience: str | None, expected: str | None) -> bool

Return True if the token's audience satisfies the configured resource URL.

RFC 8707 audience binding. expected is None disables enforcement (the binding happens upstream, e.g. at a gateway). Otherwise the comparison is exact — token audiences are URLs, not patterns — and a token carrying no audience is rejected rather than accepted, which is the whole point of configuring the canonical URL.

docs.title: bearer_challenge
docs.text:
bearer_challenge(
    *,
    resource_metadata_url: str | None,
    scopes: list[str] | None = None,
    error: str | None = None,
) -> str

Build the WWW-Authenticate value for a 401 or an insufficient-scope 403.

A backend's www_authenticate_challenge returns this, so the format is decided here once. resource_metadata_url is required by name because it is the parameter a client reads to find the authorization server (RFC 9728): a challenge missing it fails with no error on either side, and None is the explicit way to say a backend has no metadata document to point at. Pass the URL the server's protected-resource-metadata route reverses to.

The parts come in the order a client parses them: the realm, then the metadata pointer, then error, then scope (the scopes joined by a space, which is how RFC 6750 spells a scope list). A part that is None or empty is left out.

docs.title: MCPRateLimit
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

Per-binding rate limiter, evaluated after authentication and permissions.

The single consume call is the gate AND the bookkeeping update — there is no separate "check then commit" because that pattern races under concurrency. Implementations decrement quotas atomically in storage and return the suggested Retry-After in seconds once the limit is hit (0 is legal, meaning the window resets immediately), or None to allow the call.

Limiters are constructed per binding at registration time; keep them cheap to construct and thread-safe at evaluation. State that crosses requests must live in shared storage (Django cache, Redis), not on the instance, which is not shared across worker processes.

docs.title: FixedWindowRateLimit
docs.text:
A fixed-window-counter rate limiter backed by django.core.cache.

The window is bucketed by absolute time: each integer multiple of per_seconds since the epoch starts a new counter. Not as smooth as a sliding window, but it needs no sorted set.

namespace keeps multiple limits on one binding (burst plus steady-state) from sharing counters; key customises the bucket dimension and defaults to per-token-user.

The cache must be a shared backend in multi-process deployments; Django's locmem is fine for tests but enforces no global limit across worker processes.

docs.title: SlidingWindowRateLimit
docs.text:
Sliding-window rate limiter using a list of timestamps in cache.

Avoids the fixed-window edge case where a client issues 2 * max_calls requests across two adjacent windows: the timestamps of recent calls are stored in a cache entry, and each call prunes the expired ones and compares the live count against max_calls.

Trade-offs against FixedWindowRateLimit:

  • Smoother: limits the actual rate over the trailing per_seconds, not bucketed counts.
  • Memory cost: up to max_calls timestamps per key.
  • Read-modify-write: no atomic guarantee, unlike the fixed window's cache.add + cache.incr. Concurrent calls can read stale state and admit a few extra requests under contention; for strict atomicity in a multi-worker deployment, back the limiter with a Redis-Lua script.

The cache must be a shared backend in multi-process deployments; Django's locmem works for tests but shares no state across workers.

docs.title: TokenBucketRateLimit
docs.text:
Token-bucket rate limiter using Django cache for state.

A bucket holds at most capacity tokens, each accepted call consumes one, and the bucket refills continuously at refill_per_second. When empty, the limiter returns the time until one token is available again.

Trade-offs against the sliding-window scheme:

  • Burst-friendly: a full bucket absorbs capacity requests instantly, then holds the steady state at refill_per_second. Useful when consumers naturally batch.
  • Read-modify-write: like the sliding window, not strictly atomic across workers, so a few extra tokens can slip through under contention. For strict atomicity, back the limiter with a Redis-Lua script.

The cache must be a shared backend (Memcached or Redis) in multi-process deployments; Django's locmem is fine for tests but shares no state across workers.

docs.title: build_unauthenticated_response
docs.text:
build_unauthenticated_response(challenge: str) -> HttpResponse

Build a spec-compliant 401 response with the supplied WWW-Authenticate value.

The body is a small JSON envelope so MCP clients that surface error payloads to the user see a meaningful message rather than an empty body.

docs.title: build_insufficient_scope_response
docs.text:
build_insufficient_scope_response(challenge: str) -> HttpResponse

Build a 403 response signalling missing OAuth scope.

Per RFC 6750, the error="insufficient_scope" value belongs in the WWW-Authenticate header — that's already baked into challenge.

docs.title: Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728)
docs.text: The view serving the document is a plain Django view, mounted under the server's URLs as protected-resource-metadata.

docs.title: ProtectedResourceMetadataView
docs.text:
Bases: View

RFC 9728 OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata endpoint.

Mounted at /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource by MCPServer. A plain Django view answering GET, wired as ProtectedResourceMetadataView.as_view(auth_backend=...); HEAD takes the same handler and OPTIONS names the methods. The payload comes from the instance-scoped MCPAuthBackend.protected_resource_metadata, so multiple servers in one process advertise different metadata.

Open to everyone: PRM is a public discovery endpoint, so the view is CSRF-exempt and never redirected by LoginRequiredMiddleware, and the MCP transport owns its own auth pipeline through MCPAuthBackend. The answer is always JSON, because the payload shape is RFC-defined, and an Accept header admitting no JSON is refused with a 406.

docs.title: as_view
docs.text:
as_view(**initkwargs: Any) -> Callable[..., Any]

Build the view function, opted out of CSRF and of the login redirect.

The opt-outs are set as attributes, as the MCP endpoint's are, because the middleware reads them off the resolved callable.

docs.title: ProtectedResourceMetadata dataclass
docs.text:
RFC 9728 OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata payload.

Returned by MCPAuthBackend.protected_resource_metadata and serialised onto the wire by the PRM view. Keys map 1:1 to the RFC 9728 field names, except warning: a package-local extension serialised as _warning, which AllowAnyBackend uses to make dev-mode misconfiguration loud in client tooling.

docs.title: MCPServer
docs.text: register_tool registers a kernel spec as a tool, register_tools every spec in a kernel SpecRegistry, and register_resource a kernel RETRIEVE selector as a resource.

docs.title: MCPServer
docs.text:
A pluggable MCP server serving kernel specs.

The server owns its tool, resource and prompt registries, an auth backend, and a session store — all instance state, no module-level singletons. A tool or a resource is a django_service_specs spec, registered by passing it in:

from django_service_specs import SelectorKind, SelectorSpec, ServiceSpec

server = MCPServer(name="my-app")
server.register_tool(
    ServiceSpec(service=create_invoice, permissions=[IsBilling()]),
    name="invoices.create",
)
server.register_resource(
    SelectorSpec(
        kind=SelectorKind.RETRIEVE, selector=get_invoice, permissions=[IsBilling()]
    ),
    name="invoice",
    uri_template="invoices://{pk}",
)

A SpecRegistry registers in one call, register_tools, with the MCP knobs per tool in overrides.

Mount the URLs in your URL conf the admin.site.urls way — .urls is a namespaced (patterns, app_name, namespace) triple path() mounts directly (no include()):

urlpatterns = [path("mcp/", server.urls)]
# reverse("mcp:endpoint") · reverse("mcp:protected-resource-metadata")

What every spec on the mount may read -- a tenant, a locale, a clock -- is registered once as pool_seeds=, a kernel PoolSeeds:

server = MCPServer(
    pool_seeds=DEFAULT_POOL_SEEDS.extend(tenant=lambda *, user: user.tenant),
)

Every spec the server runs receives the seeds (tools over either transport, call_tool / acall_tool, task workers and resource reads), every operation condition it asks is asked with them, tools/list availability included, and a registered name is reserved: a client argument cannot occupy it, and a spec read or a URI-template variable naming it is refused at registration.

What the server tells a model in its own words -- the handle description and line, a paged tool's scope sentence, the missing-argument message -- is conventions=, an AgentConventions. Change one sentence and keep the rest:

server = MCPServer(
    conventions=AgentConventions(handle_line="Pass ids to other tools; never show them."),
)

The server still decides where each sentence appears; the conventions decide what it says, on every route the seeds above reach.

docs.title: config property
docs.text:
config: MCPConfig

This server's resolved scalars — a frozen snapshot taken at construction.

docs.title: pool_seeds property
docs.text:
pool_seeds: PoolSeeds

The pool_seeds= every dispatch and condition on this server receives.

docs.title: conventions property
docs.text:
conventions: AgentConventions

The conventions= every listing and refusal on this server is worded with.

docs.title: auth_backend property
docs.text:
auth_backend: MCPAuthBackend | None

The auth_backend= given at construction, or None when there is none.

docs.title: urls property
docs.text:
urls: tuple[list[URLPattern], str, str]

Sync URL patterns. Suitable for any deployment (WSGI or ASGI).

Returns the namespaced (patterns, app_name, namespace) triple path() mounts directly — path("mcp/", server.urls), the admin.site.urls idiom — so the endpoints reverse within the namespace (reverse("mcp:endpoint")). Use async_urls instead when running under ASGI to get non-blocking dispatch for the I/O-bound handlers.

docs.title: async_urls property
docs.text:
async_urls: tuple[list[URLPattern], str, str]

Async URL patterns for ASGI deployments.

The namespaced triple (like urls), but tools/call, resources/read and prompts/get dispatch through async-native runners. Sync collaborators (auth backend, session store, custom permissions) are bridged via asgiref.sync.sync_to_async, so a fully sync stack still works; async-native ones are detected by signature and called directly.

docs.title: register_tool
docs.text:
register_tool(
    spec: ServiceSpec | SelectorSpec,
    *,
    name: str,
    description: str | None = None,
    title: str | None = None,
    display_name: str | None = None,
    display_description: str | None = None,
    icons: tuple[Icon, ...] = (),
    annotations: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    meta: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    ui: UIToolMeta | None = None,
    content_kind: ToolContentKind = ToolContentKind.TEXT,
    content_mime_type: str | None = None,
    include_structured_content: bool | None = None,
    include_output_schema: bool | None = None,
    task_policy: TaskPolicy = TaskPolicy.FORBIDDEN,
    invalidates: tuple[str, ...] | list[str] = (),
    paginate: bool = False,
    max_page_size: int | None | UnsetType = UNSET,
    max_result_bytes: int | None | UnsetType = UNSET,
    dispatch_timeout: float | None | UnsetType = UNSET,
    always_listed: bool = False,
    rate_limits: list[Any] | None = None,
    scopes: str | Sequence[str] | None = None,
    unknown_arguments: UnknownArguments = UnknownArguments.REJECT,
    server_arguments: ServerArguments | None = None,
) -> KernelToolBinding

Register a kernel spec as a tool: a ServiceSpec or a SelectorSpec.

spec is a django_service_specs spec, and its class says which kind of tool this is. A service tool's arguments are the spec's parameters at the top level of arguments, as the kernel's spec_input_schema advertises them; a selector tool reads, and a LIST one paginates under paginate=True. The call runs through the kernel's dispatch / adispatch, which asks the spec's own permissions of the principal the auth backend resolved for the request.

Anything that is not a kernel spec is refused with a TypeError. A knob of the other kind of tool is refused: paginate / max_page_size on a service tool, invalidates on a selector tool.

A LIST selector tool registered without paginate=True warns UnboundedListWarning, and REQUIRE_LIST_PAGINATION refuses it. A paginated one whose spec declares a read named page or limit is refused, since the pagination takes both names from the arguments before the selector runs. A presenter whose audience markings cannot be projected (two labels, say) is refused naming the tool, rather than failing every tools/list of the server.

A declaration no call on this server can run as written is refused naming the tool, by the kernel's check_seeds with the server's pool_seeds: a parameter named like a registered seed or the call's own request or view, a positional-only parameter with no default, a keyword the callable requires that nothing fills, and an optional read over a keyword the callable requires. A read server_arguments binds a value to is filled on every call, so it is never refused as optional.

display_name and display_description are labels for in-process consumers, read off the binding and never sent on the wire.

scopes are the OAuth scopes the caller's token must carry, every one of them; a token missing one is answered -32006 with every declared scope in requiredScopes, as a prompt's or a view's scope gate answers. A bare string is one scope. scopes=() is refused, since it would read as a gate and admit every caller. The scope gate is a transport check and does not count as the tool's guard for REQUIRE_TOOL_PERMISSIONS, which reads the spec's own permissions.

task_policy means the same for a service tool and a selector tool: OPTIONAL answers a client that declared the tasks extension with a task handle and runs inline for one that did not, and REQUIRED refuses the latter with -32021. The spec's own checks are asked before the task is created, and the worker runs the call, under either policy, through the same dispatch a direct call takes, under the server's pool_seeds and conventions.

A refusal from dispatch is answered on the wire as kernel_refusals words it: NotPermitted and PrincipalUnavailable as -32006, InvalidArguments, ServiceValidationError and a bare DispatchError as the validation_error result, an AdditionalInputRequired as MRTR's input_required, and any other ServiceError as the service_error result.

docs.title: register_tools
docs.text:
register_tools(
    registry: SpecRegistry, *, overrides: Mapping[str, Mapping[str, Any]] | None = None
) -> tuple[KernelToolBinding, ...]

Register every kernel spec in a SpecRegistry as a tool, in order.

Each entry registers through register_tool under its registry name, with the knobs overrides holds under that name, so an entry and a direct register_tool of the same spec are the same tool. An overrides key the registry does not hold raises ValueError, as a typo rather than a no-op, and an entry that is not a kernel ServiceSpec or SelectorSpec (a SpecSource among them) is refused as register_tool refuses it. A refusal of any entry registers none of them: every entry is built and checked first.

Returns the bindings in registration order.

docs.title: call_tool
docs.text:
call_tool(
    name: str,
    arguments: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    *,
    user: Any,
    request: Any = None,
) -> ToolResult

Invoke a registered tool off the HTTP / JSON-RPC path.

The transport-neutral entry point: hand a tool name, a flat arguments dict and the acting user, and get back the same ToolResult the wire handlers build. An in-process consumer calls this instead of re-implementing dispatch.

The call runs through the kernel's dispatch as on the wire: the binding's server_arguments in place, the spec's own permissions asked of user, then the spec run and presented, a paged tool's pagination included. The transport-level checks are not consulted: the scopes= gate and rate limits read a token, and there is none in process. For those, and for tool listing, use acall_tool / list_tools.

A refusal the wire answers -32006 (NotPermitted, PrincipalUnavailable) is raised for the caller to map to its own wire; every other refusal comes back as the isError result the wire serves.

request is the caller's own Django request when there is one, and the call never writes its user to it: the spec is handed a copy whose user is user, so a view handing the request it is serving keeps serving as its own user after the call. The copy shares the handed request's body, stream and parsed POST and FILES, so a body a spec reads is read for the caller, and an object a spec mutates through it, such as META or the session, is the caller's; an attribute a spec sets or deletes changes the copy alone. With no request, a minimal POST HttpRequest bearing user is synthesised.

Raises KeyError when no tool is registered under name.

docs.title: list_tools
docs.text:
list_tools(
    cursor: str | None = None,
    *,
    user: Any,
    request: Any = None,
    scopes: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    include_unavailable: bool = False,
) -> dict[str, Any] | JsonRpcError

List the tools this server exposes, exactly as the wire would.

The in-process twin of a tools/list request: one page of the tool catalog with the same inputSchema the HTTP transport advertises (the spec's parameters, a paginated tool's page / limit and the additionalProperties policy), the same per-caller listing-permission filter (FILTER_LISTINGS_BY_PERMISSIONS) and the same opaque-cursor pagination — pass the returned nextCursor back for the next page. A JsonRpcError signals a bad cursor.

scopes are the caller's granted scopes; pass them so a tool registered with scopes= is visible under FILTER_LISTINGS_BY_PERMISSIONS exactly as it would be on the wire. A tool whose operation-scope affordances condition is unmet for user right now is left out, as on the wire, unless include_unavailable=True, which lists every tool the caller may see and asks no condition. That is for a consumer that builds its tool definitions once and asks unavailable_tools each step: it needs a definition for a tool that is unavailable when it lists and becomes available later. The wire has no such parameter.

Unlike call_tool (the spec core) this is the full transport surface. Under an event loop use alist_tools — a listing permission filter or an affordance condition that hits the DB raises SynchronousOnlyOperation from a sync call on the loop.

docs.title: alist_tools async
docs.text:
alist_tools(
    cursor: str | None = None,
    *,
    user: Any,
    request: Any = None,
    scopes: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    include_unavailable: bool = False,
) -> dict[str, Any] | JsonRpcError

Async list_tools — safe to call from an event loop.

Listing itself is pure Python, but the per-caller permission filter (FILTER_LISTINGS_BY_PERMISSIONS) and a tool's operation-scope affordances condition may each run a DB-backed check, which raises SynchronousOnlyOperation when reached synchronously from within an event loop. The whole sync handler therefore runs in Django's thread-sensitive executor.

docs.title: unavailable_tools
docs.text:
unavailable_tools(
    *, user: Any, request: Any = None, scopes: Sequence[str] | None = None
) -> dict[str, Affordance]

The tools list_tools leaves out for this caller right now, and why.

Maps each omitted tool's name to the operation-scope Affordance whose condition is unmet: its code and its reason, the sentence written for people and models alike. The answer comes from the same pass tools/list makes, over the same tools the caller may see (FILTER_LISTINGS_BY_PERMISSIONS included), so a name is here exactly when the listing omits it, and a tool hidden from this caller is never named with its reason.

For an in-process consumer that lists once with include_unavailable=True and asks this each step: it offers its model what a fresh tools/list would, and can tell the model why the rest are missing, which a listing cannot, since it only leaves them out. always_listed=True tools are never here, as they are never left out. Advisory like the listing: acall_tool still enforces every condition.

Under an event loop use aunavailable_tools; a condition or listing permission that queries raises SynchronousOnlyOperation from here.

docs.title: aunavailable_tools async
docs.text:
aunavailable_tools(
    *, user: Any, request: Any = None, scopes: Sequence[str] | None = None
) -> dict[str, Affordance]

Async unavailable_tools -- safe to call from an event loop.

Runs in Django's thread-sensitive executor, as alist_tools does, since a condition or a listing permission may query. A server none of whose tools declares an operation-scope condition answers {} without the hop: that is decided from the declarations alone, and a consumer asking on every model step should not pay a thread switch per step to learn it.

docs.title: acall_tool async
docs.text:
acall_tool(
    name: str,
    arguments: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    *,
    user: Any,
    request: Any = None,
    scopes: Sequence[str] | None = None,
) -> dict[str, Any] | JsonRpcError

Invoke a tool off the HTTP path with full transport semantics (async).

The in-process twin of a tools/call request: routes through the same async handler the wire uses, so the scopes= gate and the rate limits apply — what call_tool omits — beside the spec's own permissions and the pagination of a LIST tool. Returns the wire's result payload (a dict carrying content / structuredContent / isError), or a JsonRpcError for a protocol fault (unknown tool, malformed arguments shape, denied permission).

request is the originating Django request when there is one, handled as call_tool handles it: the call works on a copy bearing user and never writes its user to the handed request. A minimal one is synthesised otherwise. scopes populate the synthetic token so a tool registered with scopes= is invokable in-process just as it is on the wire.

docs.title: run_task
docs.text:
run_task(task_id: str) -> None

Execute a queued task. This is what a worker calls.

The other end of task_executor.enqueue, and the whole public surface of the worker side:

@shared_task
def run_mcp_task(task_id: str) -> None:
    my_server.run_task(task_id)

Everything it needs comes out of the store: the tool, the arguments, and the authorization context to re-check them under. Nothing is returned — the client learns the outcome by polling tasks/get.

Safe to call for an id that is unknown, already claimed or already finished: each is a no-op. Queues deliver at least once, and a retried delivery must not run a mutation twice.

Raises when the server has no task store: a worker calling this on a server that cannot run tasks would otherwise fail as silence — the job "succeeds" and the client polls a handle forever.

docs.title: notify_resource_updated async
docs.text:
notify_resource_updated(uri: str) -> int

Tell every subscriber watching uri that it changed.

The explicit trigger, and the one that always works. Call it from wherever the write actually happens — a management command, a Celery job, a save() override, a signal handler you wrote yourself:

await server.notify_resource_updated(f"invoices://{invoice.pk}")

Returns how many subscribers were reached — a diagnostic, not a guarantee: 0 means nobody was listening, which is the ordinary case and not an error. Notifications are best-effort by design; a client that misses one re-reads the resource.

A URI, not a template. Publish the concrete URI that changed, and the collection URI too if watchers of the collection should hear about it — matching is exact, deliberately (see topic_for_resource).

Publish after the transaction commits. Inside transaction.atomic() this announces a change that may still roll back, and a subscriber that re-reads immediately sees the old value — worse than no notification at all. transaction.on_commit is the Django-native answer.

docs.title: notify_list_changed async
docs.text:
notify_list_changed(kind: NotificationKind) -> int

Tell subscribers that one of the catalogs changed.

Registration happens once at configuration time, so the set of registered bindings is fixed for the life of the process. Two things still change a catalog under a running client: a server that registers tools from data — a plugin loader, a per-tenant catalog — and a tool whose operation-scope affordances condition flips, which tools/list answers on every request and so starts or stops listing it. Call this with TOOLS_LIST_CHANGED after the event that flipped the condition, once it has committed. It reaches only clients this server can push to: a subscription broker configured and a modern-era caller listening, the same two things listChanged is advertised on.

docs.title: register_resource
docs.text:
register_resource(
    spec: SelectorSpec,
    /,
    *,
    name: str,
    uri_template: str,
    description: str | None = None,
    title: str | None = None,
    icons: tuple[Icon, ...] = (),
    mime_type: str = "application/json",
    encoding: ResourceEncoding = ResourceEncoding.JSON,
    rate_limits: list[Any] | None = None,
    annotations: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    meta: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    always_listed: bool = False,
    cache_ttl_ms: int | UnsetType = UNSET,
    completions: dict[str, Callable[..., Any]] | None = None,
    scopes: str | Sequence[str] | None = None,
) -> KernelResourceBinding

Register a kernel RETRIEVE SelectorSpec as an MCP resource.

register_resource(spec, uri_template=..., name=...) takes a django_service_specs spec positionally. The read runs it through the kernel's dispatch / adispatch, with the URI-template variables as its arguments, so the spec's reads name them and its presenter renders the row. Anything that is not a kernel RETRIEVE SelectorSpec is refused with a TypeError. scopes gate the read as they gate register_tool.

meta is the generic _meta bundle for this resource's listing entry — resources/list for a concrete URI, resources/templates/list for a template — and for the contents block resources/read returns.

encoding decides how what the presenter returns becomes the read body. JSON pretty-prints it; TEXT returns it verbatim, and it must be a str; BLOB base64-encodes it into the contents entry's blob instead of text, and it must be bytes, bytearray or memoryview. A value of the wrong type is answered at read time as an INTERNAL_ERROR naming what produced it. Anything whose mime_type is not JSON — Markdown, CSV, plain text — wants TEXT, or the document comes back wrapped in a quoted string literal, and an image wants BLOB: a presenter rendering the row as Markdown pairs with encoding=TEXT and mime_type="text/markdown". mime_type is advertised as given and never inferred from or checked against the encoding, so TEXT left at the default application/json serves a str that is already a JSON document as it is. The result ceiling and the cache hints apply to every encoding. A TEXT or BLOB resource is refused, naming both, beside a spec declaring affordances, which the kernel adds to a presented object, or allow_none, under which a missing row presents as None without the presenter running: neither is a document or bytes. For an HTML view use register_ui_resource, which sets both.

A uri_template variable is a caller-controlled name that reaches the read's arguments, so one named after a pool seed (user, request, data …) or declared twice raises here rather than letting a URI segment stand in for the authenticated identity. So does a variable no read of the spec declares, and one the server fills for the call. A spec no read can run as written is refused naming the resource, as register_tool refuses one. A read the URI template names is filled on every read, as a value server_arguments binds is on every call, so it is never refused as optional.

A resource whose spec declares no permissions is refused for the same reason a tool is — see REQUIRE_TOOL_PERMISSIONS. The same selector exposed as a resource is as reachable as it is exposed as a tool.

docs.title: register_ui_resource
docs.text:
register_ui_resource(
    *,
    name: str,
    uri: str,
    template_name: str | None = None,
    body_template_name: str | None = None,
    diagnostics: bool | None = None,
    html: str | None = None,
    render: Callable[[], str] | None = None,
    description: str | None = None,
    title: str | None = None,
    icons: tuple[Icon, ...] = (),
    ui: UIResourceMeta | None = None,
    mime_type: str = UI_RESOURCE_MIME_TYPE,
    permissions: Sequence[PermissionCheck] | None = None,
    scopes: str | Sequence[str] | None = None,
    rate_limits: list[Any] | None = None,
    annotations: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    meta: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    always_listed: bool = False,
    cache_ttl_ms: int | UnsetType = UNSET,
) -> ResourceBinding

Register an interactive HTML view (an MCP App) as a resource.

A tool links to the view and a host renders it inline in the chat, inside a sandboxed iframe it constructs itself. The iframe and the CSP enforcement are the host's and are deliberately not implemented here.

The ui/* postMessage bridge is not in that list, and reading it as though it were is what this parameter set exists to prevent. The bridge has two ends: the host runs its end, and the document runs the other. That second end is a view's mandatory startup handshake, every one of its failure modes is silent, and one of them leaves the frame hidden with the view unable to say why.

So give exactly one content source, and prefer the first:

  • body_template_name — a Django template holding the view's markup only. The package wraps it in a document whose bridge is already written and already correct. diagnostics= decides whether that bridge writes a protocol failure into the document as well as logging it; None follows settings.DEBUG, because the text is written for whoever wrote the view and a rendered view's audience is whoever is using the product.
  • template_name — a Django template holding a whole document, whose bridge is then yours to write.
  • html — a literal document, same.
  • render — a callable returning one, which must take no arguments: one that declares a parameter is refused at registration, because the read path would fill it from a pool carrying request and user.

Keep tenant data out of the view. Hosts may prefetch and cache a view before any tool call, so it is a shell that hydrates itself at runtime from tool results — which is also why the template renders with no context.

ui= is the typed UIResourceMeta — CSP origins, browser permissions, publisher domain, border preference — which serialises into _meta under the extension's key. meta= remains available for other extensions; passing both ui= and that same key inside meta= raises, rather than letting one silently win.

The result is an ordinary ResourceBinding, so it shares one URI namespace with data resources (a collision raises as always), appears in resources/list, and honours permissions / scopes / always_listed. Views default to unguarded — the MCP session is already authenticated and a view is a static asset, not tenant data.

permissions are kernel PermissionChecks, the instances a spec carries, each asked has_permission(principal, binding) with the view's ResourceBinding as the spec; scopes are the OAuth scopes the caller's token must carry, every one, asked first. Both gate the listing, the read and a subscription alike.

docs.title: register_prompt
docs.text:
register_prompt(
    *,
    name: str,
    render: Callable[..., Any],
    description: str | None = None,
    title: str | None = None,
    icons: tuple[Icon, ...] = (),
    arguments: list[PromptArgument] | None = None,
    completions: dict[str, Callable[..., Any]] | None = None,
    permissions: Sequence[PermissionCheck] | None = None,
    scopes: str | Sequence[str] | None = None,
    rate_limits: list[Any] | None = None,
    annotations: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    meta: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
    always_listed: bool = False,
) -> PromptBinding

Register a render callable as an MCP prompt.

render receives the prompt arguments as kwargs (plus request and user if it declares them) and returns either a string, a list of strings, a list of PromptMessage, or a coroutine yielding any of those — the dispatch layer normalises the result.

request and user are seeded over the client's arguments at prompts/get, so an argument named after one of them never reaches render in the seed's place.

permissions are kernel PermissionChecks, the instances a spec carries: a prompt is not a spec, so each is asked has_permission(principal, binding) with the prompt's PromptBinding as the spec, and a check on the principal alone answers a prompt as it answers a spec. scopes are the OAuth scopes the caller's token must carry, every one, asked first; a bare string is one scope. Both gate prompts/list, prompts/get and a completion alike.

A prompt with neither is refused like a tool — see REQUIRE_TOOL_PERMISSIONS; permissions=[Unrestricted()] is the way to say it is open. A render callable reads whatever its author gave it access to, so nothing about a prompt makes it safe by construction.

meta is the generic _meta bundle for this prompt's prompts/list entry — see register_tool.

Decorator form: register the wrapped callable as a prompt.

docs.title: notify async
docs.text:
notify(session_id: str, payload: Any) -> bool

Push a JSON-RPC payload to a session's open SSE stream.

Returns True if a subscriber was present, False if no client is connected — a missed push is not generally an error, since clients pull state via tools/call round-trips. The broker enforces one subscriber per session: re-subscribing replaces the old queue silently.

With a SSEReplayBuffer configured the payload is recorded before publishing, so the frame carries an event ID the SSE generator emits on the wire (id: <id> data: <payload> ) and a later reconnect with Last-Event-ID drains what it missed before resuming live mode. Without a buffer there are no id: lines and resume is disabled.

Multi-process deployments need an out-of-process broker to fan out across workers; the in-process broker only sees its own.

docs.title: AgentConventions dataclass
docs.text:
The sentences this server writes for a model, one field per sentence.

Passed as MCPServer(conventions=...), per server, because two servers in one project can be talking to different readers. AgentConventions() is the default, and its fields carry the wording a server uses when it is given none; change one field and every other sentence stays the package's, so a later correction to a line you did not override still reaches you.

The server still decides whether each sentence appears: a tool with no handle gets no handle line, a tool that returns no page no scope sentence. A field changes what it says, never when. None drops a sentence where dropping one leaves a well-formed answer.

Every field is a str.format template, rendered wherever it lands whether or not it has a placeholder, so a literal brace is written twice, {{ or }}, in every field alike. The placeholders a field accepts are the ones listed on it, and only missing_arguments accepts one. Anything the server could not render raises ImproperlyConfigured naming the field when the conventions are built, so a typo fails when the server is, rather than inside the first call that reaches it. This is the Pydantic-AI toolset's rule for its AgentConventions, so one template reads the same on both transports.

Some of these sentences state facts about how the server behaves: that a selection applies to each item and never to the envelope, that the envelope's keys are items, page, totalPages and hasNext. Wording you supply owns keeping those facts true.

Raises:

Type Description ImproperlyConfigured

A field uses a placeholder it does not accept, is not a valid format string, cannot be rendered with the values it will be given ({names:q}), is neither a string nor None, or is missing_arguments set to None or to an empty or whitespace-only string.

docs.title: handle_field_description class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
handle_field_description: str | None = HANDLE_DESCRIPTION

The outputSchema description of a handle field that declares none of its own, beside the field in every tool's output schema. None leaves such a field undescribed. A FieldMarking.handle("...") keeps its own words whatever this says. No placeholders.

docs.title: handle_line class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
handle_line: str | None = HANDLE_LINE

The line appended to the description of a tool whose output carries a handle, after Identify records by `<label>`. when the presenter declares a label. None drops the line and that prefix with it. No placeholders.

docs.title: query_param_on_pages class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
query_param_on_pages: str | None = PAGED_QUERY_PARAM_SCOPE

What a read-shaping parameter, one of a spec's shapes, applies to on a tool that returns a page. Appended to the param's description in the tool's inputSchema, and to the isError message when a value it supplied is refused while that tool's result is rendered. None drops it from both. No placeholders.

docs.title: missing_arguments class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
missing_arguments: str = MISSING_ARGUMENTS

The message of a validation_error result for a call that left out arguments the tool's selectors cannot run without: a selector parameter with no default or a service tool's target lookup. {names} is the missing names, sorted, each in backticks, joined with ", "; the detail stays keyed by each name. A validator's own refusal, a missing field included, keeps "Invalid arguments". Never None, empty or only whitespace: it is the result's whole message.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
The JSON encoder and the ToolResult builder.

A tool's result has two halves and they are toggled independently: structuredContent on the call result, and outputSchema on the tools/list entry. The MCP spec imposes one asymmetric rule between them — a tool that advertises outputSchema must return conforming structuredContent, while the reverse is allowed — so they are not a single switch.

Both are on by default, server-wide via SPEC_MCP["INCLUDE_STRUCTURED_CONTENT"] and ["INCLUDE_OUTPUT_SCHEMA"], and per tool via include_structured_content= and include_output_schema= at registration. The asymmetric rule is enforced: include_output_schema=True with include_structured_content=False raises at registration rather than advertising a schema nothing will satisfy.

That is a check on the settings, not on a response. To assert that a real result satisfies the schema its tool advertised — types and formats, not only the property names — see assert_tool_result_conforms.
